Cognitive Psychology · Theme 3 · Problem 3

Autobiographical memory, amnesia & photo-taking

Childhood amnesia, the reminiscence bump, the self-memory system, amnesia and the kinds of memory, and what taking photos does to memory: every concept, study and example

Dear Sezen,

Problem 3 asks one big question from three angles: how do we hold on to our own past? Part A looks at healthy autobiographical memory: why the first years are missing, how we pull a personal memory out, why some memories stick and how the whole system is organised. Part B looks at what breaks when the brain is damaged, and what that teaches us about different kinds of memory. Part C brings it into your pocket: what happens to memory when you take a photo instead of just looking.

How to read this platform. The Lessons panel has three tabs: 📖 Full lectures (33 screens, reading by reading: Robinson-Riegler, Eysenck & Keane, Baddeley et al. with Matlin, and Soares & Storm), 🎯 Learning objectives (A1–A5, B1–B4, C1–C3, each with a model answer) and 🧠 In-depth questions (the 17 tutorial questions A1–A6, B1–B5, C1–C6, each with triage and a hidden model answer). On every screen look at the diagram first, read the bullets, say the hook out loud, then open the chips. Numbers marked ≈ are read off figures; anything illustrative only shows a shape.

— Your professor

🗄️ The big picture in one paragraph: Think of your autobiographical memory as a personal archive run by a librarian. The archive has shelves at different levels: broad chapters of your life (“my school years”), general events (“Saturday football”) and single vivid scenes (“the goal I scored in the rain”). The librarian is your working self: your current goals and self-image decide what gets filed and what gets fetched. Part A studies the archive and the librarian. Part B studies patients whose archive stopped accepting new files (anterograde amnesia) or lost old ones (retrograde amnesia), yet who can still use information without knowing they have it (implicit memory). Part C asks whether a camera acts as a second archive that makes the librarian lazy.

🧵 Synthesis

One thread runs through all three parts: memory is built around the self and its goals. In Part A, the working self decides what is encoded and retrieved, and childhood amnesia ends when a self emerges. In Part B, amnesia shows that the ‘glue’ binding an event to me, here, then (the hippocampus) can fail while facts and skills survive. In Part C, a camera changes how engaged the self is in the moment, and memory suffers.

Exam tip: link the parts. For example, source amnesia (B3) explains why childhood memories may be borrowed from family photos (A1, A5), and transactive memory (C1) is a social version of the working self deciding what is worth storing internally.

One thread links A, B and C: memory depends on binding an experience to its context, and anything that disrupts that binding costs memory. In healthy memory, the working self decides what is bound and kept, so memories drift toward coherence with our goals (A5, A6), and the tools for binding (brain, self, language) explain why infancy is missing and young adulthood over-represented (A4). In amnesia, the hippocampal ‘glue’ is damaged, so patients keep items and skills but lose the where and when (B1, B3), rely on familiarity instead of recollection (B4), and lose fragile new traces to interference (B5). In healthy people, photo-taking may disrupt the same encoding of the experience, not because the camera stores it for us, but because our attention and effort drop (C3, C5).

Part A · Robinson-Riegler (pp. 268–279)
Lecture 1 of 33 · objectives A4

🎞️ Autobiographical memories and autobiographical facts

Recalling a life: episodes and personal knowledge

  • Autobiographical memory (a type of episodic memory): memory for one’s own life experiences, a specific event in time and place.
  • Autobiographical fact (a type of semantic memory): a piece of general knowledge about oneself (‘I was born in Ankara’).
  • Memory for events seems to move from episodic to semantic: first a distinct episode, then, with much repetition, general knowledge.
  • Linton (1975): repeated episodes lose their individual character and become autobiographical facts.
  • Both kinds live together in autobiographical memory, and both appear in every method that studies it.
🪝 Memory hook: Memory = a film clip 🎞️; fact = an index card 📇.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Autobiographical memory mixes re-lived episodes with personal facts, and repetition turns episodes into facts.
Tap to open ▸
Remembering the day your sister was born, with the smells and sounds, is an autobiographical memory. Just knowing you have a sister is an autobiographical fact. Do something often enough and the clips merge into a fact.
Autobiographical memoryAutobiographical fact
Memory systemepisodicsemantic
Contentone event, time and placegeneral knowledge about me
Feels likere-livingknowing
Examplethe evening my sister was bornI have a younger sister

🧩 Comprehension check

Is ‘I went to primary school in Rotterdam’ a memory or a fact?

An autobiographical fact: general personal knowledge without re-living a specific event.

Why do routine events become facts?

Repeated episodes blend together and lose their individual character (Linton, 1975).

Part A · Robinson-Riegler (pp. 268–279)
Lecture 2 of 33 · objectives A5

🔬 How to study autobiographical memory

Targeted event recall, diaries and the Galton–Crovitz technique

  • Targeted event recall: specific questions about a particular event or period of life; checkable events allow accuracy to be verified.
  • Diary technique: participants record a number of events each day for a period; memory for them is tested later.
  • Galton–Crovitz cue-word technique (revived by Crovitz & Schiffman, 1974): word cues are presented, participants retrieve a memory for each, describe it and date it.
  • The cue-word method lets researchers see the autobiographical memory retention function: the distribution of personal memories across the life span.
  • Main problem for early memories: there is often no way to check whether someone remembers the event or a story or photo of it.
🪝 Memory hook: Target 🎯, diary 📔, cue word 🔤: aim, record, or prompt.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Each method trades verifiability against breadth; cue words map a whole life but can’t be checked.
Tap to open ▸
You can ask people about a specific event you can check, have them keep a diary and quiz them later, or give them words like ‘river’ and see what memories pop up and when they happened.
MethodProcedureStrengthLimitation
Targeted event recallquestions about one event or periodverifiable (records, relatives)few events; contamination by stories and photos
Diaryrecord daily events, test lateraccuracy knowneffortful; selective; small samples
Galton–Crovitz cue wordsword cue → memory → date itwhole life span; retention functiondates and content unverifiable

🧩 Comprehension check

Which method produces the retention function?

The Galton–Crovitz cue-word technique (participants date memories cued by words).

What is the main methodological problem with early childhood memories?

There is usually no way to check whether a memory is real or reconstructed from family stories and photos.

Part A · Robinson-Riegler (pp. 268–279)
Lecture 3 of 33 · objectives A3 · A5

📈 The retention function across the life span

Childhood amnesia, the reminiscence bump and forgetting

  • Rubin, Wetzler & Nebes (1986) used the cue-word technique with participants aged 18–76 to plot memories by age at encoding.
  • 1 · Childhood amnesia: very few memories from early life and almost none before about age 3.
  • 2 · Reminiscence bump: a disproportionate number of memories from ages 10 to 30.
  • 3 · A standard forgetting curve for the last ~20 years (visible in older participants): most recalled events are recent.
  • Explaining this function has occupied autobiographical-memory researchers for years: the next lectures take each part in turn.
🪝 Memory hook: Dip – bump – slope 📉📈📉: nothing early, lots in your twenties, and recent stuff.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The life-span retention function has three signature parts, each needing its own explanation.
Tap to open ▸
If you ask a 70-year-old for memories to random words, almost none come from before age 3, a big pile comes from their teens and twenties, and the rest are mostly from the last few years.
ComponentAge rangePhenomenon
Childhood amnesia0 to about 3 (few before 10)almost no memories
Reminiscence bump10–30more memories than expected
Forgettinglast ~20 yearsrecent events best, steady decline

🧩 Comprehension check

Why is the forgetting part visible only in older participants?

Only they have a long enough span since early adulthood for a separate recency segment to appear.

Name the three phenomena of the retention function.

Childhood amnesia, the reminiscence bump and a standard forgetting curve for recent decades.

Part A · Robinson-Riegler (pp. 268–279)
Lecture 4 of 33 · objectives A1 · A5

🧸 Childhood amnesia: evidence from checkable events

Usher & Neisser (1993)

  • Childhood amnesia: a steep drop in memories before age 10 and none before 2–3; ‘offset of childhood amnesia’ = ‘emergence of autobiographical memory’.
  • To avoid unverifiable memories, Usher & Neisser (1993) used targeted, documented events: sibling birth, family move, death, hospitalisation.
  • Typical pattern: relatively poor memory before age 5, but the offset differs by event: sibling birth and hospitalisation go back further than a death or a move.
  • Hospitalisation: distinctive, involving, frightening. Sibling birth: the first instalment of a story retold again and again (rehearsal).
  • Rehearsal is complex: at ≤ 3 years, more stories and photos meant fewer own memories (fragile memories overwritten); at 4–5 they helped.
🪝 Memory hook: Hospital 🏥 and new baby 👶 beat moving boxes 📦.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The end of childhood amnesia depends on the event, and rehearsal helps only once memories are sturdy enough.
Tap to open ▸
Some early events stick because they were scary and unusual, or because the family keeps telling the story. But if you were very small, the stories can replace your own memory instead of strengthening it.
📄 Usher & Neisser (1993)
ElementDetail
QuestionWhen do memories of documented early events begin?
MethodParticipants answered questions about sibling birth, family move, death and hospitalisation, checkable with relatives; rehearsal and photo exposure were also asked
Findingspoor memory before age 5; sibling birth and hospitalisation remembered from earlier ages; rehearsal helped only for events at age 4–5
Conclusionthe offset of childhood amnesia varies with the event
Why it mattersdistinctiveness and retelling shape early memory

🧩 Comprehension check

Why might hospitalisation be remembered from an early age?

It is distinctive, involving and frightening, which makes it highly memorable.

Why can family stories reduce memories of events at age 3 or younger?

The child’s own memory is fragile and may be overwritten by the stories and photos.

Part A · Robinson-Riegler (pp. 268–279)
Lecture 5 of 33 · objectives A1

🧠 Explanation 1: brain development

Necessary but not sufficient

  • Infant hippocampus (critical for new long-term memories) is underdeveloped (Nadel & Zola-Morgan, 1984; Squire, 1987); the prefrontal cortex develops rapidly around age 1.
  • Link to amnesic patients: hippocampal damage spares learning of skills (procedural) but not new events (declarative).
  • Proposal (Bachevalier & Mishkin, 1984; Schacter & Moscovitch, 1984): infants first have an early procedural system; a later declarative system supports autobiographical memory.
  • Problem 1: this explains amnesia only for very early events, not for ages 3–4.
  • Problem 2: children don’t show childhood amnesia: 2–3-year-olds recall events from age 1–2 (Bauer, 2004), so the basic machinery is there.
🪝 Memory hook: The hardware is installed 💻, but the life story isn’t being saved yet.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Brain maturation is needed for autobiographical memory but can’t by itself explain childhood amnesia.
Tap to open ▸
Maybe babies’ brains just aren’t ready to store memories? Partly. But toddlers can tell you about things from months ago, so the brain can store them. It’s just that those memories don’t last into adulthood.
ClaimEvidenceProblem
Hippocampus immatureNadel & Zola-Morgan (1984)amnesia lasts until 3–4
Prefrontal development ~1 yrDiamond & Doar (1989)toddlers do recall earlier events
Procedural before declarativeBachevalier & Mishkin (1984)at best oversimplified
▶ autobiographical memory childhood amnesia explained▶ reminiscence bump explained(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

Which finding casts most doubt on a purely neurological account?

Young children can recall events from when they were even younger (Bauer, 2004), so the machinery exists.

What does ‘necessary but not sufficient’ mean here?

Brain maturity is required for autobiographical memory, but other factors are also needed to explain the amnesia.

Part A · Robinson-Riegler (pp. 268–279)
Lecture 6 of 33 · objectives A1

💬 Explanation 2: language and memory talk

Elaborative vs pragmatic reminiscing

  • Language account: children remember events as soon as they can describe them in words; the biggest language strides happen between ages 2 and 4.
  • Parents reminisce in different styles (Fivush; Reese & Fivush, 1993): elaborative (long, richly detailed accounts) vs pragmatic (less detail).
  • Children of elaborative parents give more detailed accounts of past events.
  • Style is linked to the child’s sex; Davis (1999) found female superiority in autobiographical memory.
  • Nelson (1993): autobiographical memory starts when parents engage in memory talk, acting as guides to what happened, how and why.
🪝 Memory hook: Talk it, keep it 🗣️📦.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Rich parent–child memory talk helps children turn experiences into lasting, retellable memories.
Tap to open ▸
Kids whose parents chat with them about the past in rich detail (‘What did the elephant do? How did you feel?’) end up with earlier and fuller memories, because talking turns a moment into a story.
Elaborative stylePragmatic style
Talk about the pastlong, richly detailed, questionsshort, little detail
Child’s accountsmore detailedless detailed
Linkmore common with girls?Davis (1999): female superiority
▶ autobiographical memory childhood amnesia explained▶ reminiscence bump explained▶ elaborative reminiscing parents children memory(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

What is the difference between an elaborative and a pragmatic reminiscing style?

Elaborative parents give long, richly detailed accounts and ask questions; pragmatic parents give short accounts with little elaboration.

According to Nelson (1993), when does autobiographical memory begin?

When parents begin to engage in memory talk with their children.

Part A · Robinson-Riegler (pp. 268–279)
Lecture 7 of 33 · objectives A1

🪞 Explanation 3: a cognitive self, shaped by culture

Howe & Courage (1997); Wang (2006)

  • Howe & Courage (1997): language expresses experiences but is not the same as storing them; an 18-month-old may know what happened without being able to say it.
  • The critical factor is a developing sense of self: knowing you are a unique person who thinks and acts; it organises autobiographical experiences. Language ‘lets memories out’.
  • Wang (2006): US and Taiwanese adults recalled earliest memories to cues (self, mother, family, friend, surroundings).
  • US participants had earlier memories for all cues and more autonomous content; Taiwanese memories were more social (independent vs interdependent self; Markus & Kitayama, 1991).
  • ‘Mother’ cues gave especially early memories in both cultures: the mother–child relationship is central to the developing autobiography.
🪝 Memory hook: No ‘me’ yet = no ‘my memories’ 🪞.
★ KEY INSIGHT · A sense of self organises autobiographical memory, and culture shapes both when it starts and what it contains.
Tap to open ▸
To have memories of your life, you first need to know there is a ‘you’. Cultures that stress the individual get people talking about ‘me’ earlier, and their first memories come earlier and are more about themselves.
📄 Wang (2006)
ElementDetail

MethodUS and Taiwanese adults gave their earliest memory for the cues self, mother, family, friend, surroundings; age at event and autonomy were coded
FindingsUS memories earlier for all cues and more autonomous; Taiwanese memories more relational; ‘mother’ gave especially early memories in both
Conclusionemphasis on an independent self brings earlier, self-focused memories

🧩 Comprehension check

What role does language play according to Howe and Courage?

It is the mechanism by which memories are expressed (‘let out’), not the basis of their development; the self is the key factor.

What did Wang (2006) find for the cue ‘mother’?

It led to especially early memories in both cultures, reflecting the centrality of the mother–child relationship.

Part A · Robinson-Riegler (pp. 268–279)
Lecture 8 of 33 · objectives A1 · A3

🎙️ Jack et al. (2009): mother–child talk predicts first memories

The first prospective study

  • Prospective design: over two years (child aged 2–4), mothers recorded natural conversations about six events from the previous four months, without researchers present.
  • Coding: elaborations (new topic or aspect) vs repetitions (verbatim or simple rephrasing).
  • Ten years later, the adolescents reported their earliest childhood memory.
  • A strong negative correlation between the elaboration/repetition ratio and the age of the earliest memory: more elaborative mothers → earlier first memories.
  • Together with Wang (2006) and others (Davis, 1999; Wang & Ross, 2007): cultural and social interaction shapes the developing life story.
🪝 Memory hook: Elaborate today, remember from earlier tomorrow 🧩.
★ KEY INSIGHT · How parents talk about the past with toddlers predicts how far back their memories reach as adolescents.
Tap to open ▸
Researchers had mums tape their chats with toddlers, then waited ten years. Kids whose mums added new details instead of just repeating themselves later remembered further back in their lives.
📄 Jack, MacDonald, Reese & Hayne (2009)
ElementDetail
QuestionDoes early maternal reminiscing affect later autobiographical memory?
MethodMothers taped conversations about past events when children were 2–4; elaborations and repetitions were coded; 10 years later adolescents gave their earliest memory
Findingsstrong negative correlation: higher elaboration-to-repetition ratio → earlier earliest memory
Conclusionelaborative memory talk helps memories form and last
Why it mattersprospective evidence for the language/social account
▶ autobiographical memory childhood amnesia explained▶ reminiscence bump explained(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

Why is a prospective design stronger here?

Maternal talk was measured before the outcome, ten years earlier, so it can’t be biased by the adolescents’ later memories.

What does a negative correlation mean in this study?

The higher the elaboration ratio, the lower (earlier) the age of the earliest memory.

Part A · Robinson-Riegler (pp. 268–279)
Lecture 9 of 33 · objectives A1

🧵 Explanation 4: the social-cognitive account

Nelson & Fivush (2004) and the ‘wane’ at 4.7 years

  • Brain, language and self all play a role: Nelson & Fivush (2004) weave them together and stress emergence: there is no single moment when memories switch on.
  • Ingredients: basic explicit memory (by ~2; Bauer, 2004), language and narrative, memory talk with adults, a sense of self across time (extended consciousness, ~age 4; Povinelli et al., 1999) and theory of mind.
  • Because these develop at different times for different people, the offset is disputed: 2–2.5 (Eacott & Crawley, 1998; Usher & Neisser) vs about 5 (Wetzler & Sweeney, 1986).
  • Multhaup, Johnson & Tetrick (2005): childhood memories shift gradually from ‘know’ to ‘recollect’ (remember–know paradigm).
  • The point where most memories are recollected, the ‘wane of childhood amnesia’, is around 4.7 years, with large individual variation.
🪝 Memory hook: Autobiographical memory is a rope 🪢 of five strands, not a light switch 💡.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Autobiographical memory emerges gradually from several developing abilities, which is why its starting age varies.
Tap to open ▸
There isn’t a birthday on which your memory turns on. Brain growth, words, chatting with parents, knowing you’re the same ‘me’ over time, and understanding other minds all come together slowly, around age four or five.
📄 Multhaup, Johnson & Tetrick (2005)
ElementDetail
QuestionWhy do estimates of the offset differ?
MethodParticipants recalled childhood events and labelled each as ‘know’ or ‘recollect’
Findingsmemories shift gradually from known to recollected; most become recollected at about 4.7 years, with large individual differences
Conclusionthe end of childhood amnesia is a gradual wane, not a cut-off
Why it mattersfits the social-cognitive account

🧩 Comprehension check

What is ‘extended consciousness’ and why does it matter?

A sense of a past self connected to the present self, appearing around age four; it is needed to experience memories as ‘my past’.

Why do estimates of the end of childhood amnesia differ (2 vs 5 years)?

Methods differ, and memories shift gradually from know to recollect with large individual variation.

Part A · Robinson-Riegler (pp. 268–279)
Lecture 10 of 33 · objectives A3

🎓 The reminiscence bump

Ages 10–30 are over-represented: in memories, tastes and knowledge

  • People recall disproportionately many memories from ages 10–30; an intuitive reason: many firsts and milestones (first kiss, job, college).
  • But Rubin, Rahhal & Poon (1998) showed a bump also for autobiographical facts such as preferences, and for public events seen as important.
  • Songs popular when people were 10–30 are preferred (Holbrook & Schindler, 1989); memorable books were read at 10–40 (Larsen, 1996); similar for films (Schulster, 1996).
  • General semantic knowledge too: questions on Academy Awards, World Series and news were answered best for early adulthood (Figure 7.4); recent events were also fairly good.
  • So the ‘firsts’ explanation alone is not enough: the next lecture weighs the accounts.
🪝 Memory hook: Your twenties play on repeat 🎵: memories, music and facts.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The bump covers personal events, preferences and general knowledge, so it needs a broader explanation than ‘firsts’.
Tap to open ▸
Ask older people about their lives, their favourite songs or even quiz questions, and their teens and twenties win every time. It isn’t only about exciting firsts: even facts from that period stick better.
DomainFindingSource
Personal eventsmore memories from 10–30Rubin, Wetzler & Nebes (1986)
Musicsongs from 10–30 preferredHolbrook & Schindler (1989)
Booksmemorable reading at 10–40Larsen (1996)
Public knowledgebest for early adulthoodRubin, Rahhal & Poon (1998)

Why do the music and knowledge findings challenge the ‘firsts’ explanation?

They show the bump for preferences and general facts, not just for novel personal milestones.

What did Rubin, Rahhal and Poon (1998) test?

Multiple-choice knowledge of public events (Academy Awards, World Series, current events) from across the life span.

Part A · Robinson-Riegler (pp. 268–279)
Lecture 11 of 33 · objectives A3

🔍 Explaining the reminiscence bump

Cognitive, identity and peak-functioning accounts

  • Cognitive-mechanisms account: events of early adulthood are important and distinctive, so they are rehearsed often and suffer little interference.
  • Identity account: adolescence to early adulthood is when identity forms (Erikson, 1950); Habermas & Bluck (2000), ‘Getting a life’: the tools and motives for a coherent life story develop in adolescence. Parallel to the cognitive-self account of childhood amnesia.
  • Peak-functioning account: brain and cognition peak in early adulthood. Janssen & Murre (2008): ~3,500 participants; a clear bump even for ordinary, unemotional, unimportant events.
  • Reconciliation: as we age, novel, emotional and important events are rehearsed at the expense of mundane ones, so cognitive and identity factors explain different forgetting rates.
  • Brain development: necessary but not sufficient for the end of childhood amnesia; necessary and sufficient for the bump.
🪝 Memory hook: The bump = a peak-performance camera 📸 that’s also writing your life story 📖.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The bump likely reflects peak encoding in early adulthood, with identity and rehearsal shaping which memories survive later.
Tap to open ▸
Maybe teen and twenty-something memories stick because that’s when big stuff happens, when you figure out who you are, or simply because your brain is at its best. A huge online study found even boring memories from then stick, so ‘peak brain’ matters a lot.
📄 Janssen & Murre (2008)

🧩 Comprehension check

Why did Janssen and Murre’s results favour the peak-functioning account?

Bump memories were ordinary rather than novel, emotional or important, so their advantage must come from better encoding at that age.

How does the identity account parallel the cognitive-self account of childhood amnesia?

Childhood events are encoded better once we know THAT we are; later events once we know WHO we are.

Part A · Robinson-Riegler (pp. 268–279)
Lecture 12 of 33 · objectives A3

⏳ Forgetting autobiographical memories

A standard forgetting curve and its causes

  • For the period just before recall there is a standard forgetting curve: recent events are remembered well, then recall drops quickly.
  • Wagenaar (1986), a diary study: recall fell from nearly 75% to under 33% over four years, the same pattern as Ebbinghaus’s classic curve.
  • Causes: lack of rehearsal; interference between similar episodes; routine events that blend together and become autobiographical facts (Linton, 1975).
  • Culture affects specificity: Euro-Americans tend to remember specific episodes, Asian and Asian-American people more generic memories (Wang & Ross, 2007; Wang, 2009).
  • So forgetting completes the retention function: amnesia, bump, then the recency slope.
🪝 Memory hook: Unused, crowded, routine 🗂️ = forgotten.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Autobiographical forgetting follows the classic curve, driven by lack of rehearsal, interference and routine.
Tap to open ▸
Most of last month is already blurry, because the days were similar, you didn’t talk about them and they crowd each other out. Only the unusual ones survive.
CauseExplanation
Lack of rehearsalevents not thought about or discussed fade
Interferencemany similar episodes compete at retrieval
Routinerepeated events become autobiographical facts
Culturespecific vs generic memory styles
▶ autobiographical memory childhood amnesia explained▶ reminiscence bump explained▶ Wagenaar diary study forgetting(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

What did Wagenaar (1986) find?

Recall of diary events fell from about 75% to under 33% over four years.

Why is the last part of the retention function called a ‘standard forgetting curve’?

It has the classic shape found since Ebbinghaus: recent events best, then a decline with time since the event.

Part B · Eysenck & Keane (pp. 314–320)
Lecture 13 of 33 · objectives A3

📜 The bump revisited: life scripts and identity

Eysenck & Keane’s view

  • Life-script account: we share a cultural script of expected life events (graduation, marriage) that cluster in early adulthood and guide retrieval.
  • Support: the bump is much stronger for positive than negative memories, as expected if scripted, mostly happy events are retrieved.
  • Problem: unexpected personal events also show a strong bump, less consistent with a script guiding retrieval.
  • Identity account: our strongest memories are those most relevant to self-identity (Conway, 2005), which develops in adolescence and early adulthood.
  • Conclusion: the late teens and twenties differ from other periods in many ways (identity, novel experiences), so several factors contribute.
🪝 Memory hook: Script 📜 + self 🪪 + firsts ✨ = the bump.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The bump fits life scripts and identity formation, but unexpected events show it too, so several factors combine.
Tap to open ▸
Part of why your twenties stand out is that your culture tells you what should happen then (graduating, marrying), and part is that those years made you who you are. No single reason covers it all.
AccountPredictionEvidence
Life scriptbump for expected, positive eventsbump stronger for positive memories ✓
no bump for unexpected eventsunexpected events also show a bump ✗
Self-identityself-defining memories strongestidentity develops in adolescence ✓

Which finding supports the life-script account?

The bump is much stronger for positive than for negative memories.

Which finding is a problem for it?

Part B · Eysenck & Keane (pp. 314–320)
Lecture 14 of 33 · objectives A2 · A4

🏛️ The self-memory system model

A hierarchical knowledge base steered by the working self

  • Two components (Conway & Pleydell-Pearce, 2000): the autobiographical memory knowledge base and the working self.
  • Knowledge base levels: lifetime periods (substantial times defined by ongoing situations), general events (repeated or single), event-specific knowledge (images, feelings, details, usually in temporal order).
  • Conway (2005) added the life story (general factual and evaluative knowledge about ourselves) and themes (major domains such as work, relationships) at the top.
  • The working self holds the self, what it may become, and current goals; its goals influence what is stored and what we recall.
  • So autobiographical memories are ‘primarily records of success or failure in goal attainment’.
🪝 Memory hook: An archive 🗄️ with a librarian 🎯 who files by your goals.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Autobiographical memory is a goal-driven system: a hierarchical knowledge base under the control of the working self.
Tap to open ▸
Your life memories are stored like a filing cabinet: big drawers for life chapters, folders for typical events, and the actual photos and feelings inside. A librarian, your current goals and self-image, decides what gets filed and fetched.
LevelContentExample
Life storygeneral factual and evaluative self-knowledge‘I am someone who moved a lot’
Themesmajor life domainswork, relationships

General eventsrepeated or single extended eventsweekly hockey; trip to Australia

What are the two components of the self-memory system?

The autobiographical memory knowledge base and the working self.

What does the working self do?

It holds current goals and self-images and influences what is encoded and retrieved.

Part B · Eysenck & Keane (pp. 314–320)
Lecture 15 of 33 · objectives A4

🧩 Coherence over correspondence: evidence for the model

KC, retrograde amnesia and Woike et al. (1999)

  • Conway (2005): we want memories to show coherence (consistency with current goals and beliefs) and correspondence (accuracy); over time coherence tends to win.
  • So memories are often inaccurate: people recall past selves negatively to feel they have improved (Newman & Lindsay, 2009); this can enhance self-image and relationships.
  • Retrograde amnesia: episodic memories are hit hard, general events and lifetime periods less so. KC had no episodic memories but some general autobiographical knowledge (Rosenbaum et al., 2005); self-knowledge about personality is resilient.
  • Woike et al. (1999): agentic people (independence, achievement) vs communal people (interdependence, love, friendship) recalled a positive or negative experience.
  • Positive: 65% of agentic people recalled agentic memories, 90% of communal people communal ones; negative: 47% vs 90% → memories match the working self’s motives.
🪝 Memory hook: Memory edits for a good story 🎬, not a court record ⚖️.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Memory serves the self: coherence beats accuracy, and recall follows personal motives.
Tap to open ▸
Your memory cares more about fitting who you are now than about being exact. Achievement-driven people remember their successes and failures; relationship-driven people remember love and betrayal.

Part B · Eysenck & Keane (pp. 314–320)
Lecture 16 of 33 · objectives A2

🔎 Generative vs direct retrieval

Two routes, with behavioural and brain evidence

  • Generative retrieval: deliberate, effortful construction of memories by combining working-self resources with the knowledge base; often tied to the person’s goals.
  • Direct retrieval: involuntary, triggered by a specific cue (hearing ‘Paris’ on the radio); less effortful, no working self needed.
  • Uzer, Lee & Brown (2012): think-aloud recall to emotion words: direct retrieval about three times faster, with less vocalisation.
  • Johannessen & Berntsen (2010): direct memories more specific but less significant and less relevant to identity → working self more involved in generative retrieval.
  • Addis et al. (2012): generative → more prefrontal activity (strategic search); direct → more left hippocampus.
🪝 Memory hook: Generative = searching the library 🔎; direct = a book falling off the shelf 📕.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Memories are reached either by goal-guided search or directly by a cue, with different speed, content and brain activity.
Tap to open ▸
Sometimes you dig for a memory step by step (‘that summer… the trip… the beach’). Other times a song plays and a memory just appears. The second is way faster.
GenerativeDirect
Controldeliberate, effortfulspontaneous, involuntary
Working selfinvolvednot involved
Speed (Uzer et al., 2012)slower≈ 3× faster
Contentmore significant, identity-relevantmore specific

Why would direct retrieval be faster?

It skips the step-by-step search: a cue activates event-specific knowledge directly.

What did Johannessen and Berntsen (2010) find?

Directly retrieved memories were more specific but less significant and less relevant to identity than generative ones.

Part B · Eysenck & Keane (pp. 314–320)
Lecture 17 of 33 · objectives A2

🧬 Cognitive neuroscience of autobiographical memory

Prefrontal cortex, amygdala and four networks

  • The prefrontal cortex plays a major role: meta-analysis (Svoboda et al., 2006): medial and ventromedial PFC, plus medial and lateral temporal cortex.
  • Summerfield et al. (2009): only real (not imagined) autobiographical events activated the ventromedial PFC and posterior cingulate.
  • Autobiographical memories are often emotional; the amygdala is involved, and amygdala damage makes emotional memories harder to retrieve (Buchanan et al., 2006; Markowitsch & Staniloiu, 2011).
  • St Jacques et al. (2011): four networks: fronto-parietal (controlled construction), cingulo-opercular (goal maintenance), medial PFC (self-reference), medial temporal lobe (recollection).
  • All four help construct a memory, with strong two-way connections; only medial PFC and medial temporal lobe support later elaboration.
🪝 Memory hook: Construct 🏗️ then elaborate 🎨: four networks build it, two paint it in.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Autobiographical retrieval is a network process with distinct construction and elaboration phases.
Tap to open ▸
Remembering your life isn’t one brain spot lighting up. Several networks work together to find the memory, and then a couple of them fill in the details and the feelings.
NetworkRole
Fronto-parietaladaptive controlled processing in construction
Cingulo-operculargoal maintenance during construction
Medial prefrontalself-referential processing; construction + elaboration
Medial temporal lobedeclarative memory, conscious recollection; construction + elaboration
▶ self memory system Conway autobiographical memory▶ generative vs direct retrieval autobiographical memory(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

Which brain structure links emotion and autobiographical retrieval?

The amygdala: patients with amygdala damage find emotional autobiographical memories harder to retrieve.

Which networks support elaboration?

Only the medial prefrontal cortex and medial temporal lobe networks.

Part B · Eysenck & Keane (pp. 314–320)
Lecture 18 of 33 · objectives A3 · A4

🌧️ Depression and over-general memories

Specificity, vulnerability and recovery

  • The self-memory system predicts that stored memories reflect a person’s personality and sense of self, so depression should change autobiographical memory.
  • Task: recall a specific memory (< 1 day) to a cue word. Depressed people give over-general memories: ‘angry’ → ‘arguing with people’ (meta-analysis: Liu et al., 2013).
  • Most evidence is only correlational. Stronger: in adolescents, over-general memory predicted increased depressive symptoms eight months later in those with high familial emotional abuse.
  • Longitudinal: increased specificity predicted recovery from major depression (Brittlebank et al., 1993).
  • Affect regulation hypothesis: over-general memory as cognitive avoidance of painful specific memories; threat instructions increased over-generality only in avoidant copers (Debeer et al., 2011).
🪝 Memory hook: Depression blurs the photos 🌫️ to avoid the painful close-ups.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Over-general memory accompanies, predicts and may maintain depression, possibly as avoidance.
Tap to open ▸
Asked for a time they felt angry, a depressed person may say ‘arguing with people’ rather than one particular day. Staying vague may protect them from painful details, but it also keeps them stuck.
FindingSourceStrength of evidence
Depressed people give over-general memoriesLiu et al. (2013), meta-analysiscorrelational
Over-generality predicts later symptoms (with emotional abuse)adolescent study (2013)longitudinal
Specificity predicts recoveryBrittlebank et al. (1993)longitudinal
Avoidance increases over-generalityDebeer et al. (2011)experimental (threat instructions)

🧩 Comprehension check

What is an over-general memory?

A summary of repeated or extended events (‘arguing with people’) instead of a specific event lasting less than a day.

What does the affect regulation hypothesis claim?

Over-general retrieval is a cognitive avoidance strategy that protects people from intense negative emotions linked to specific memories.

Part B · Eysenck & Keane (pp. 314–320)
Lecture 19 of 33 · objectives A4

🗂️ Depression and the structure of autobiographical knowledge

Dalgleish et al. (2011) and conclusions

  • Dalgleish et al. (2011): patients with current major depression, patients in remission and controls listed their lifetime periods (about 9–10 each) and chose positive and negative words for each.
  • Measures: proportion negative, compartmentalisation (how much negativity varies across periods), positive and negative redundancy (same terms reused across periods).
  • Current patients: far more negative terms, more compartmentalisation (a less integrated self), partly due to low positive redundancy.
  • Remitted patients were intermediate: recovery involves a ‘healthier’ view of one’s history, but their more negative, less integrated view suggests risk of relapse.
  • EK conclusions: over-general memories in depression partly reflect avoidant coping; they mirror a negative, poorly integrated self; over-generality increases risk and specificity predicts recovery.
🪝 Memory hook: A depressed life story is a book with dark, disconnected chapters 📕.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Depression shows up in how autobiographical knowledge is organised: more negative and less integrated.
Tap to open ▸
When people with depression map their life into chapters, more chapters are labelled negatively and the chapters don’t hang together. People who have recovered sit in between.
📄 Dalgleish et al. (2011)
ElementDetail
QuestionHow is autobiographical knowledge organised in depression?
MethodCurrent MDD, remitted MDD and healthy controls listed lifetime periods and chose positive and negative items for each
Findingscurrent patients: more negative items, greater compartmentalisation, low positive redundancy; remitted patients intermediate
Conclusiondepression goes with a negative, poorly integrated self-structure
Why it mattersfits the self-memory system: memory structure reflects the self

What does high compartmentalisation mean?

The proportion of negative items varies a lot across lifetime periods, indicating a less integrated sense of self.

Why might remitted patients still be at risk?

Their life-structure was still more negative and less integrated than controls’.

Part C · Baddeley et al. (438–445) & Matlin (146–147)
Lecture 20 of 33 · objectives B4

🧠 The amnesic syndrome: anterograde and retrograde

What is lost and what is spared

  • Most cognitive problems across many diseases stem from impaired episodic memory; the pure amnesic syndrome shows this clearly.
  • Anterograde amnesia: problem encoding, storing or retrieving new information for future use. Retrograde amnesia: problem accessing events from before the damage.
  • HM: classic dense anterograde amnesia; earlier memories largely intact. Clive Wearing: dense anterograde plus very patchy retrograde. A patient studied by Wilson & Baddeley (1988) had dense anterograde amnesia without retrograde amnesia.
  • In its pure form: grossly impaired episodic memory with preserved working memory, semantic memory, implicit memory and intelligence.
  • In practice amnesia often comes with other deficits, but the episodic deficit is usually central to the patient’s problems.
🪝 Memory hook: Retrograde ◀ looks back, anterograde ▶ looks forward.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The amnesic syndrome isolates episodic memory: new or old events are lost while other memory systems remain.
Tap to open ▸
Brain damage can wipe out memories from before (retrograde) or stop new ones being saved (anterograde). People with pure amnesia can still chat, know facts and learn skills; they just can’t keep new experiences.
TypeDirectionExample
Anterogradecan’t lay down new episodes after damageHM; Leonard in Memento
Retrogradecan’t access episodes from before damageClive Wearing (with anterograde)
Pure syndrome sparesworking memory, semantic, implicit, intelligence—

🧩 Comprehension check

What is the difference between anterograde and retrograde amnesia?

Anterograde: inability to form new memories after the damage. Retrograde: loss of access to memories from before the damage.

Which abilities are spared in the pure amnesic syndrome?

Working memory, semantic memory, implicit memory and intelligence.

Part C · Baddeley et al. (438–445) & Matlin (146–147)
Lecture 21 of 33 · objectives B1 · B2

🧩 Explicit vs implicit memory: a dissociation

Warrington & Weiskrantz (1970)

  • Explicit memory: conscious remembering, tested by recall and recognition. Implicit memory: earlier experience changes performance without conscious recollection.
  • Warrington & Weiskrantz (1970) gave people with anterograde amnesia a word list: on recall and recognition they did much worse than controls.
  • Implicit test, presented as word-guessing: identify words in mutilated (fragmented) form. Both groups were correct 45% of the time.
  • Replicated with visual and auditory tasks (Roediger & Amir, 2005; Schacter et al., 1994), with some exceptions (Reder et al., 2009).
  • A dissociation: a variable (amnesia) has a large effect on one kind of test but little or none on another → memory is not one thing.
🪝 Memory hook: Can’t tell you, can still show you 🤐✍️.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Amnesia impairs explicit memory but spares implicit memory: a classic dissociation showing separate memory systems.
Tap to open ▸
Amnesic patients can’t remember seeing a list of words, yet when they guess half-erased words, they’re just as good as healthy people at filling in those same words. Part of memory works without awareness.
📄 Warrington & Weiskrantz (1970)
ElementDetail
QuestionIs all memory impaired in amnesia?
MethodAmnesic patients and controls saw English words, then explicit tests (recall, recognition) and an implicit word-guessing test with fragmented words
Findingspatients much worse on explicit tests; both groups 45% on the implicit test
Conclusionexplicit and implicit memory dissociate
Why it mattersclassic evidence for multiple memory systems

Part C · Baddeley et al. (438–445) & Matlin (146–147)
Lecture 22 of 33 · objectives B3 · B4

📅 Explaining amnesia: the context-binding deficit

Huppert & Piercy (1978)

  • Early hypotheses: susceptibility to interference (Warrington & Weiskrantz, 1970), faster forgetting (Huppert & Piercy, 1979), inability for deep processing (Cermak et al., 1974); all ran into problems, though they may still play a part.
  • Likely: amnesia disrupts the ability to associate an episode with its context, its location in time and place.
  • Rats with hippocampal lesions were poor at using environmental context (Winocur & Mills, 1970), suggesting this might apply to humans (Winocur, 1978).
  • Huppert & Piercy (1978a, b): pictures shown once or twice on each of two days (patients given longer to encode, to equate recognition). Asked which day: patients judged pictures seen twice on day 1 as from day 2; controls did the opposite.
  • Without a contextual link, patients relied on familiarity, which can’t tell ‘seen twice’ from ‘seen recently’.
🪝 Memory hook: Patients judge by brightness ✨, not by date stamp 📅.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The focal deficit in amnesia is binding items to context, leaving only familiarity to guide judgements.
Tap to open ▸
Without the brain’s ‘date stamp’, a picture you saw twice feels very familiar, so you guess you saw it most recently. Healthy people remember when they saw it.
📄 Huppert & Piercy (1978a, 1978b)
ElementDetail
QuestionDo amnesic patients lose memory for context?
MethodPictures shown once or twice on day 1 and day 2 (patients had longer encoding); then recognition plus ‘which day?’
Findingspatients said pictures seen twice on day 1 came from day 2; controls more accurate for twice-shown day-1 pictures
Conclusionpatients use familiarity, not the link to context
Why it mattersevidence for a context-binding deficit
▶ anterograde amnesia explained▶ amnesia HM Clive Wearing(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

Why did patients attribute twice-seen day-1 pictures to day 2?

They relied on familiarity, and greater familiarity (from two presentations) felt like recency.

Why were patients given longer to encode the pictures?

To roughly equate overall recognition between groups, so differences in day judgements reflect context memory.

Part C · Baddeley et al. (438–445) & Matlin (146–147)
Lecture 23 of 33 · objectives B3 · B4

🔎 Source amnesia and imagining the future

Schacter et al. (1984); Hassabis et al. (2007)

  • Schacter, Harbluk & McLachlan (1984): trivia answers (e.g. comedian Bob Hope’s favourite food) given to amnesic patients.
  • Patients could recall the ‘fact’ but not that they had just been given it, confusing recency with familiarity: source amnesia.
  • Tulving: episodic memory allows ‘mental time travel’. Amnesic patients struggle with the recent past, and with the future too.
  • Imagining a sandy tropical beach: patients could imagine the components but not integrate them into a whole (Hassabis, Kumaran, Vann & Maguire, 2007), reflecting the hippocampus’s role in spatial processing.
  • Mullally & Maguire (2013): the hippocampus supports both episodic memory and imagination, but these are best seen as separate functions.
🪝 Memory hook: Fact without its label 🏷️❌; future without a scene 🧩.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Without context binding, facts lose their source, and scenes, past or future, can’t be assembled.
Tap to open ▸
Amnesic patients can learn a trivia fact but think they always knew it. And when asked to imagine a beach holiday, they can name the sand and palms but can’t build the whole scene.
📄 Schacter, Harbluk & McLachlan (1984)

Part C · Baddeley et al. (438–445) & Matlin (146–147)
Lecture 24 of 33 · objectives B2 · B4

🧴 A simplified ‘modal model’ of amnesia

Mnemonic glue

  • Baddeley’s modal model tried to capture most of the amnesia data with an unspecified consolidation hypothesis.
  • Episodic learning = associating items with their context using some form of ‘mnemonic glue’, giving each experience a contextual tag for later retrieval.
  • Consistent with the contextual hypothesis of amnesia.
  • Assumptions: recall and recognition use the same storage processes, and semantic memory is the residue of many episodes.
  • Plausible, but hard to test; then a patient, Jon, convinced Baddeley the model was wrong, or far too simple.
🪝 Memory hook: Memory = item + context, stuck with glue 🧴.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The modal model treats amnesia as a failure to glue items to context, with semantic memory built from episodes.
Tap to open ▸
Baddeley’s simple idea: to remember an event, your brain glues it to when and where it happened. In amnesia the glue fails. But one boy, Jon, didn’t fit this picture.
AssumptionProblem raised by Jon
Semantic memory = residue of episodesJon has poor episodic memory but good semantic memory
Crystallised intelligence depends on prior learningJon has above-average intelligence and vocabulary
Recall and recognition share storageJon: recall impaired, recognition normal

🧩 Comprehension check

What does ‘mnemonic glue’ refer to?

An unspecified process that binds an experience to its specific context, so it can later be retrieved.

Name two assumptions of the modal model.

Recall and recognition rely on the same storage processes; semantic memory is the residue of many episodes.

Part C · Baddeley et al. (438–445) & Matlin (146–147)
Lecture 25 of 33 · objectives B2 · B4

👶 Jon and developmental amnesia

Recall vs recognition; remembering vs knowing

  • Jon was born prematurely; breathing problems (anoxia) damaged his hippocampus (less than half normal size), apparently the limit of the damage. Memory problems were noticed at about 5.
  • Despite amnesia, he developed above-average intelligence and good semantic memory (though he may take longer to learn new facts; Gardiner et al., 2008).
  • Doors and People test (Baddeley, Vargha-Khadem & Mishkin, 2001): recall clearly impaired, recognition within the normal range.
  • Remember/know: Jon used ‘remember’ as often as controls but described no recollection: he judged by the strength of a visual image → he lacks the remember component (MEG: Düzel et al., 2001).
  • Maguire et al. (2001) found a few re-lived memories with the normal ‘remember’ brain pattern: he can recollect, but has great difficulty laying down episodic traces.
🪝 Memory hook: Jon knows ✔️ but rarely remembers 🎞️.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Jon shows that recognition, semantic learning and intelligence can survive early hippocampal damage that devastates recall and recollection.
Tap to open ▸
Jon lost most of his hippocampus as a newborn. He can’t recall much, but he recognises things normally, went to school, and knows lots of facts. He seems to run on a feeling of ‘I’ve seen this’ rather than re-living.

Recall (Doors and People)clearly impaired
Recognitionwithin normal range

🧩 Comprehension check

Which three assumptions of the modal model does Jon challenge?

That semantic memory needs episodes, that intelligence/vocabulary would suffer, and that recall and recognition share the same storage.

How did Jon decide something was ‘remembered’?

By how clear and bright his visual image of the word was: a strength criterion rather than recollection.

Part C · Baddeley et al. (438–445) & Matlin (146–147)
Lecture 26 of 33 · objectives B2

🔬 Recollection vs familiarity

Why is Jon different? Aggleton & Brown, Squire, Horner et al.

  • Most amnesic patients are impaired on both recall and recognition. Why is Jon different?
  • Possibility 1: very early (developmental) damage; current research doesn’t support this, but it can’t be ruled out.
  • Possibility 2: damage limited to the hippocampus with perirhinal and entorhinal cortex spared. Aggleton & Brown (1999): hippocampus → recollection; perirhinal → familiarity-based recognition. Mayes et al. (2002): an adult case like Jon.
  • Counter: Squire’s patients with hippocampus-limited lesions showed no preserved recognition (Reed & Squire, 1997; Manns & Squire, 1999).
  • Horner et al. (2012): 17 patients, 14 controls; hippocampal volume predicted context memory but hardly item memory; an early (~350 ms) MEG signal linked to context. Promising, but not yet settled.
🪝 Memory hook: Hippocampus = the movie 🎞️; perirhinal = the feeling of ‘seen it’ ✨.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Recognition may rest on two processes in different structures, but whether hippocampal damage spares familiarity is still debated.
Tap to open ▸
Recognising something can happen two ways: you re-live where you saw it, or it just feels familiar. Jon lost the first but kept the second, which is why he can recognise but not recall.
📄 Horner et al. (2012)
ElementDetail
QuestionDoes the hippocampus support context rather than item memory?
Method17 relatively pure amnesic patients and 14 controls saw words on scenes; tests of item memory (word seen?) and context memory (with which scene?); MEG during retrieval
Findingshippocampal volume had minimal effect on item memory but a clear effect on context memory; an early (350 ms) hippocampus-dependent signal tracked context
Conclusionthe hippocampus binds items to context
Why it matterssupports Aggleton & Brown, though the issue isn’t fully resolved
▶ anterograde amnesia explained▶ amnesia HM Clive Wearing(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

According to Aggleton and Brown, which structure supports familiarity?

The perirhinal cortex adjacent to the hippocampus.

Why don’t Squire’s patients fit Jon’s pattern?

Their hippocampus-limited damage impaired both recall and recognition (though subtle wider damage can’t be excluded).

Part C · Baddeley et al. (438–445) & Matlin (146–147)
Lecture 27 of 33 · objectives B4

🛌 Consolidation

Why rest after learning helps amnesic patients

  • Dominant neurobiological explanation of both amnesias: consolidation: memory traces are fragile at first and become resistant over time (Müller & Pilzecker, 1900), depending on the hippocampus.
  • Sleep after learning improves retention (Stickgold et al., 2000; Gaskell & Dumay, 2003).
  • Dewar, Cowan & Della Sala (2010): an hour in a quiet, darkened room after a story → amnesic patients almost as good as controls; the same hour filled with assessment tasks → virtually nothing. Similar for MCI patients.
  • Dewar et al. (2009): interference in the first part of a 9-minute delay caused most forgetting → early consolidation is most vulnerable.
  • Consolidation probably works at the cellular level via long-term potentiation (LTP); potentially important for practice and assessment.
🪝 Memory hook: New memories are wet paint 🎨: don’t touch them straight away.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Amnesic patients suffer most from early interference during consolidation; rest after learning protects new memories.
Tap to open ▸
Right after learning, a memory is fragile. For people with amnesia, doing other tasks straight away wipes it out, but resting quietly in a dark room lets it settle almost as well as in healthy people.
📄 Dewar et al. (2009)

Why do assessment tasks after learning hurt amnesic patients so much?

They provide interference during early consolidation, when new traces are most fragile.

What mechanism probably underlies consolidation at the cellular level?

Long-term potentiation (LTP).

Part C · Baddeley et al. (438–445) & Matlin (146–147)
Lecture 28 of 33 · objectives B4 · A5

⏪ Retrograde amnesia

Ribot’s law, measurement and dissociations

  • Retrograde amnesia: impaired retrieval of old memories; often especially severe for the years just before the damage (Matlin: L.T. lost events before her accident; memory after it was normal).
  • Ribot’s law (1882): older memories are more durable; famous-faces test (Sanders & Warrington, 1971) showed earlier memories better preserved.
  • Public-event scales (news, horse races, one-season TV shows; Squire et al., 1989) have two problems: knowledge varies across people, and scales age.
  • Alternative: autobiographical recollections checked with a spouse (Zola-Morgan et al., 1983): laborious. The Autobiographical Memory Interview (Kopelman, Wilson & Baddeley, 1990) probes personal semantic memory and specific incidents per life period; valid even in Korsakoff patients.
  • Anterograde and retrograde severity are not highly correlated (Shimamura & Squire, 1991): two pure amnesics differed hugely in retrograde memory (Baddeley & Wilson, 1986); De Renzi et al. (1987): personal events fine, public events lost.
🪝 Memory hook: Ribot: the oldest bricks 🧱 are the sturdiest.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Retrograde amnesia follows a temporal gradient and is hard to measure; its severity dissociates from anterograde amnesia.
Tap to open ▸
When brain damage takes old memories, it usually takes the most recent ones first, because older memories have had more time to set. Testing this is tricky because you rarely know what someone originally learned.
MethodIdeaProblem
Famous faces / news eventstest public knowledge by decadeknowledge varies; scales age
Autobiographical recollection + informantcheck memories with spouselaborious, hard to score
AMI (Kopelman et al., 1990)personal facts + incidents per life periodstill effortful, but reliable and valid
▶ anterograde amnesia explained▶ amnesia HM Clive Wearing▶ retrograde amnesia Ribot's law(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

What does Ribot’s law state?

Older memories are more durable than recently acquired ones, so recent memories are lost first.

Why are public-event tests problematic?

People differ in how much they knew about public events, and the test items keep ageing.

Part D · Soares & Storm (2018)
Lecture 29 of 33 · objectives C1 · C2

📸 Photos, memory and transactive memory

Henkel (2014) and the offloading hypothesis

  • Photos are powerful retrieval cues (e.g. SenseCam; Loveday & Conway, 2011), and photo-taking could help encoding (isolation; deeper, more varied processing).
  • But Henkel (2014): on a museum tour, photographed objects were remembered less well than observed ones: the photo-taking-impairment effect.
  • Transactive memory (Wegner, 1987): a shared memory system; couples split remembering (Wegner, Erber & Raymond, 1991). It extends to objects: notes, computers (Sparrow, Liu & Wegner, 2011), the Internet.
  • Offloading frees resources for other tasks (Storm & Stone, 2015), but offloaded information is less recallable when the partner is unavailable.
  • Offloading hypothesis: people rely on the camera’s ‘prosthetic memory’ instead of their own ‘organic’ memory (Risko & Gilbert, 2016).
🪝 Memory hook: The camera as your memory spouse 💍📷: it remembers, so you don’t.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Henkel’s photo-taking-impairment effect was first explained as offloading memory to the camera as a transactive partner.
Tap to open ▸
Couples split remembering: one does birthdays, the other bills. Maybe we treat our phone camera the same way: ‘I don’t need to remember this painting, I’ve got a photo.’

What is transactive memory?

A shared memory system in which people (or people and objects) divide remembering and know who or what holds which information.

What is the photo-taking-impairment effect?

Objects that are photographed are remembered less well than objects that are only observed (Henkel, 2014).

Part D · Soares & Storm (2018)
Lecture 30 of 33 · objectives C3

⚖️ Offloading vs attentional disengagement

The logic of Soares & Storm (2018)

  • Attentional-disengagement hypothesis: people disengage from the moment to handle photo-taking, so they encode less deeply, during and perhaps after taking the photo.
  • Support: Niforatos et al. (2017) found the effect only for manually taken photos, not with an automatic wearable camera; Mols et al. (2015): people feel more disengaged when photographing a trip.
  • Key assumption: encoding suffers automatically, whether or not the camera is a reliable memory partner.
  • Critical test: a condition where people take photos but can’t rely on them. Offloading predicts the impairment disappears; disengagement predicts it stays.
  • Soares & Storm used a lab version of Henkel’s paradigm: paintings on a computer screen.
🪝 Memory hook: Offloading = ‘camera remembers’ 🗄️; disengagement = ‘camera distracts’ 👀.
★ KEY INSIGHT · A no-save photo condition pits the two hypotheses against each other.
Tap to open ▸
If people forget because they trust the camera, making the photo disappear should fix it. If they forget because using the camera pulls their attention away, a disappearing photo won’t help.
HypothesisMechanismPrediction for Snapchat / Delete
Offloadingreliance on the camera’s prosthetic memoryimpairment eliminated or reduced
Attentional disengagementphoto-taking disrupts encoding automaticallyimpairment as large as with Camera

What would the offloading hypothesis predict when photos aren’t saved?

That the photo-taking impairment should be eliminated or greatly reduced, because people can’t rely on the camera.

What did Niforatos et al. (2017) find?

The impairment occurred only for manually taken photos, not those taken automatically by a wearable camera.

Part D · Soares & Storm (2018)
Lecture 31 of 33 · objectives C2 · C3

👻 Experiment 1: Snapchat

Impairment even when photos vanish

  • 42 UCSC undergraduates, within-subjects: Observe, Camera (saved to album) and Snapchat (sent, not saved); 15 paintings, 15 s each; Latin-square counterbalancing.
  • Told they could use the phone at test (Camera photos only). After a 10-minute Tetris delay: a 30-item multiple-choice test on visual details (chance .25).
  • Main effect: F(2, 82) = 15.35, p < .001, ηp² = .27. Camera < Observe (d = 0.70): the effect replicated.
  • Against offloading: Snapchat also impaired memory (d = 1.21) and was even worse than Camera (d = .48).
  • Caution: viewing time was 15 s in all conditions, so Snapchat may have cut looking time; participants may not have believed photos would vanish.
🪝 Memory hook: Disappearing photo, still disappearing memory 👻.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Photo-taking impaired memory even without a saved photo, against the offloading hypothesis, but time and belief were confounds.
Tap to open ▸
Even when people knew their snaps would vanish, they remembered the paintings worse than when they just looked. If they weren’t counting on the photo, ‘offloading’ can’t be the whole story.

Why was Snapchat a clever manipulation?

It lets people take photos without expecting the camera to save them, so offloading should not occur.

Name the two limitations of Experiment 1.

Less viewing time in the Snapchat condition (fixed 15 s) and possible disbelief that photos would vanish.

Part D · Soares & Storm (2018)
Lecture 32 of 33 · objectives C2 · C3

🗑️ Experiment 2: Delete

Time controlled, deletion certain

  • Fixes: Delete condition (photo deleted immediately, so participants surely knew it was gone) and viewing time controlled: the 15 s timer started after the photo.
  • 51 participants (power analysis: ≥ 49 for 90% power), within-subjects, otherwise as Experiment 1.
  • Main effect F(2, 100) = 4.26, p = .017, ηp² = .08. Camera < Observe (d = 0.58); Delete < Observe (d = 0.61); Camera = Delete (p = .80).
  • So even with equal or more viewing time and no photo to rely on, memory was impaired.
  • Survey (31 participants): 52% believed photos help memory, 26% no effect, 3% unsure, 19% impairment; 62.5% of believers still remembered less.
🪝 Memory hook: Deleted photo, deleted details 🗑️.
★ KEY INSIGHT · With time controlled and photos deleted, the impairment remained: offloading cannot explain it, and people misjudge the effect.
Tap to open ▸
This time people deleted each photo and still got 15 full seconds to look. They still remembered less, and most thought taking photos helps memory.

Part D · Soares & Storm (2018)
Lecture 33 of 33 · objectives C3

💡 General discussion: what explains the effect?

Disengagement, metacognitive illusion, implicit offloading

  • An impairment appeared in every photo condition, even when photos weren’t saved → inconsistent with explicit offloading.
  • More consistent with attentional disengagement, which apparently continues even after the camera is put down (Exp. 2).
  • Speculative: a metacognitive illusion: photo-taking gives a sense of encoding fluency, so people put in less effort afterwards (Bjork, Dunlosky & Kornell, 2013).
  • Or implicit/automatic offloading: a learned transactive habit with cameras that runs even when people know the photo is gone; it might itself cause disengagement.
  • Open: would any secondary task do this? Photos here were instructed; volitional photography can boost engagement and memory (Diehl et al., 2016; Barasch et al., 2017). Photos help only if reviewed (Whittaker et al., 2010).
🪝 Memory hook: Not ‘the camera remembers’ but ‘the camera distracts’ 📵.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Explicit offloading is out; disengagement, possibly via a metacognitive illusion or automatic offloading, best fits, within the limits of instructed lab photos.
Tap to open ▸
The best guess is that taking a photo pulls you slightly out of the moment, and you stay a bit checked out afterwards, maybe because it feels like you already ‘got it’. Choosing what to photograph yourself may be different.

Attentional disengagementyesimpairment despite extra viewing time
Metacognitive illusionpossiblysense of having encoded → less effort; survey beliefs
Implicit offloadingpossiblyhabit can run despite knowing photos are gone
