🧩 Comprehension check

Why can’t the authors rule out implicit offloading?

People may automatically treat photographed information as stored elsewhere through learned experience, even when they consciously know it isn’t.

Why does it matter that photos were instructed?

When people choose what to photograph (volitional photography), photo-taking can increase engagement and memory, so the effect may not generalise.

🧵 Synthesis

One thread runs through all three parts: memory is built around the self and its goals. In Part A, the working self decides what is encoded and retrieved, and childhood amnesia ends when a self emerges. In Part B, amnesia shows that the ‘glue’ binding an event to me, here, then (the hippocampus) can fail while facts and skills survive. In Part C, a camera changes how engaged the self is in the moment, and memory suffers.

Exam tip: link the parts. For example, source amnesia (B3) explains why childhood memories may be borrowed from family photos (A1, A5), and transactive memory (C1) is a social version of the working self deciding what is worth storing internally.

One thread links A, B and C: memory depends on binding an experience to its context, and anything that disrupts that binding costs memory. In healthy memory, the working self decides what is bound and kept, so memories drift toward coherence with our goals (A5, A6), and the tools for binding (brain, self, language) explain why infancy is missing and young adulthood over-represented (A4). In amnesia, the hippocampal ‘glue’ is damaged, so patients keep items and skills but lose the where and when (B1, B3), rely on familiarity instead of recollection (B4), and lose fragile new traces to interference (B5). In healthy people, photo-taking may disrupt the same encoding of the experience, not because the camera stores it for us, but because our attention and effort drop (C3, C5).

Part A · Autobiographical memory
🎯 Learning objective · A1
❓ The question this screen answers
A1
Why don't we have memories from when we were babies?

🧭 In plain words: Describe childhood (infantile) amnesia and weigh the explanations. The mark is in the evaluation: which account fits which evidence, and why no single account is enough.

  • Offset ~2–5 years depending on method
  • Brain maturation is necessary, not sufficient (Bauer, 2004)
  • Elaborative talk → earlier memories (Jack et al., 2009)
  • Culture shifts the offset (Wang, 2006)
  • Best account: social-cognitive emergence (Nelson & Fivush, 2004)
🪝 Memory hook: A baby is like a camera with no memory card format yet: it sees everything, but the files are not saved in a format your adult computer can open.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Childhood amnesia is not a storage failure of the baby alone; it is the absence of the tools (language, self, narrative) that turn an experience into a retrievable personal memory.
Tap to open ▸

Childhood amnesia is the near-absence of adult memories for events from the first years of life. Estimates of the ‘offset’ differ with the method: around age 2–2.5 when people are asked about specific checkable events (Usher & Neisser, 1993; Eacott & Crawley, 1998), up to about age 5 with free cue-word recall (Wetzler & Sweeney, 1986). Multhaup, Johnson and Tetrick (2005) showed a gradual shift from ‘know’ to ‘remember’ judgements, with the amnesia waning at about 4.7 years. Usher and Neisser also showed that some events (birth of a sibling, a hospitalisation) are remembered from earlier ages than others (a death, a move).

Four explanations are offered. (1) Brain development: the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex are immature in infancy (Nadel & Zola-Morgan, 1984), so infants may rely on procedural rather than declarative memory. But 2–3-year-olds can recall events from age 1–2 (Bauer, 2004), so maturation is necessary but not sufficient. (2) Language: memories are stored and retold in words. Children whose mothers use an elaborative style (rich questions, extending the story) rather than a pragmatic one develop earlier and richer memories (Reese & Fivush, 1993). Jack, MacDonald, Reese and Hayne (2009) recorded mother–child talk at age 2–4; ten years later, a higher ratio of elaborations to repetitions predicted earlier first memories. (3) Cognitive self (Howe & Courage, 1997): until about age 2 there is no ‘me’ to organise experiences around; language only ‘lets memories out’. (4) Culture: Wang (2006) found that American adults report earlier first memories than Taiwanese adults, linked to an emphasis on the autonomous individual and on talking about personal past.

The best-supported view is the social-cognitive (emergent) account (Nelson & Fivush, 2004). Autobiographical memory is not switched on at one moment. It emerges from basic memory (present by age 2), language, memory talk with parents, a sense of self, and at around age 4 an understanding that past events belong to a continuous ‘me’ (extended consciousness, theory of mind). Until these pieces are in place, early events are not stored in a form an adult can retrieve as my past.

  • Stating only one explanation without evaluation.
  • Saying babies have ‘no memory’: infants learn and remember (imitation, recognition); what is missing is autobiographical recall.
  • Forgetting the counter-evidence to the brain account (2-year-olds recall events from age 1).

Part A · Autobiographical memory
🎯 Learning objective · A2
❓ The question this screen answers
A2
How do we retrieve memories of personal events?

🧭 In plain words: Explain the two retrieval routes in the self-memory system (generative vs direct), give evidence for their differences, and name the brain networks involved.

  • Generative = goal-driven, effortful, working self
  • Direct = cue-driven, fast (~3×, Uzer et al., 2012)
  • Direct memories: more specific, less self-relevant
  • Generative: more prefrontal; direct: more hippocampal (Addis et al., 2012)
  • Construction phase then elaboration phase
🪝 Memory hook: Generative retrieval is searching your phone gallery by scrolling year → month → day; direct retrieval is a ‘memory from 5 years ago’ notification.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Most everyday autobiographical memories are direct: they come to us. Lab studies with cue words mostly measure the generative route.
Tap to open ▸

Conway and Pleydell-Pearce (2000) distinguish two routes. Generative retrieval is deliberate and effortful. Guided by the working self (current goals), we search the autobiographical knowledge base step by step: from a lifetime period (‘when I lived in Istanbul’) to a general event (‘summer evenings on the ferry’) to event-specific knowledge (the smell, the conversation), checking each candidate against the retrieval goal. Direct retrieval is spontaneous: a cue in the environment (hearing ‘Paris’ on the radio) activates event-specific knowledge directly, and a memory pops up without a search.

Evidence supports the distinction. Uzer, Lee and Brown (2012) asked people to think aloud while recalling memories to emotion cues: direct retrievals were about three times faster and involved less verbalised search. Johannessen and Berntsen (2010) found that directly retrieved memories were more specific but less significant and less tied to identity than generative ones, as expected if the working self steers only generative search.

Neuroimaging shows retrieval is a network process. Addis et al. (2012) found more prefrontal activation during generative retrieval (strategic search and monitoring) and more left hippocampal activation during direct retrieval. St Jacques, Kragel and Rubin (2011) identified four interacting networks: fronto-parietal, cingulo-opercular, medial prefrontal and medial temporal. A meta-analysis (Svoboda et al., 2006) confirms a core of medial/ventromedial prefrontal and medial/lateral temporal cortex. Retrieval unfolds in two phases: construction (finding the memory) and elaboration (filling in details), with emotional memories depending on the amygdala (Buchanan et al., 2006).

  • Describing retrieval as a single look-up rather than a reconstructive search.
  • Mixing up the terms: ‘generative’ is the effortful one.
  • Leaving out evidence (Uzer et al.; Addis et al.).

Part A · Autobiographical memory
🎯 Learning objective · A3
❓ The question this screen answers
A3
Why are some memories more memorable than others?

🧭 In plain words: Explain the factors that make memories last (distinctiveness, emotion, rehearsal, self-relevance) and the reminiscence bump, including its competing explanations.

  • Reminiscence bump: ages 10–30
  • Four accounts: cognitive, identity, life script, peak functioning
  • Distinctive, emotional, rehearsed, goal-relevant events last
  • Routine events merge into general knowledge
  • Culture shapes content and specificity
🪝 Memory hook: Your 18–25 playlist still gets stuck in your head; your 40-year-old parents’ playlist is also from their 18–25. That is the bump.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Memorability is not only about the event; it is about the fit between the event and the self that remembers it.
Tap to open ▸

When older adults recall memories to cue words, the retention function shows three parts: childhood amnesia, a reminiscence bump for ages 10–30, and a recency effect (Rubin, Wetzler & Nebes, 1986). The bump also appears for favourite songs, books and films, and for general knowledge (Rubin, Rahhal & Poon, 1998). Four accounts compete. The cognitive account says the period is full of novel, distinctive ‘firsts’ that are rehearsed and suffer little interference. The identity account says this is when the adult self forms (Erikson; Habermas & Bluck, 2000), so self-defining events are kept. The life-script account says we remember best the culturally expected events (graduation, marriage), which cluster in these years; the bump is stronger for positive than negative events, which fits. The peak-functioning account (Janssen & Murre, 2008) found the bump in about 3,500 online participants even for events that were not novel, emotional or important, suggesting the brain simply encodes best in these years.

Beyond age, memorability depends on: distinctiveness (a hospitalisation is unusual and frightening, so it is remembered from early ages; Usher & Neisser, 1993); emotion, supported by the amygdala; rehearsal (retelling strengthens memories, while routine events blend into general knowledge: Linton, 1975; Wagenaar, 1986, whose recall fell from about 75% to under a third over four years); and self-relevance. Conway and Pleydell-Pearce (2000) argue that autobiographical memories are ‘primarily records of success or failure in goal attainment’, so events that matter for the working self are retained. Culture also shapes what is kept: Euro-Americans recall more specific self-focused episodes, Asians more generic and social memories (Wang & Ross, 2007).

  • Naming the bump without explaining it.
  • Listing accounts without evidence for/against (e.g., positive > negative supports life script).
  • Forgetting that repeated routine events become semantic.

Part A · Autobiographical memory
🎯 Learning objective · A4
❓ The question this screen answers
A4
How does autobiographical memory work? What kind of information does it contain and how is it organized?

🧭 In plain words: Define autobiographical memory, describe the self-memory system (knowledge base + working self), and give evidence and limitations.

  • Episodic + semantic (autobiographical facts)
  • Hierarchy: life story → themes → lifetime periods → general events → episodes
  • Working self: goals control encoding & retrieval
  • Coherence beats correspondence
  • Evidence: amnesia, KC, Woike et al., depression
🪝 Memory hook: Like a Netflix series: seasons (lifetime periods), recurring plotlines (general events), and single unforgettable scenes (episodes). You are both the main character and the editor.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Autobiographical memory is organised for the self, not for accuracy. It is a story we keep editing.
Tap to open ▸

Autobiographical memory is memory for the events of one’s own life. It combines episodic content (specific experiences with time and place) and semantic content (autobiographical facts such as where I was born). With repetition, episodes can turn into autobiographical facts (Linton, 1975).

The most influential model is the self-memory system (Conway & Pleydell-Pearce, 2000; Conway, 2005). It has two parts. The autobiographical knowledge base is organised hierarchically: the life story and themes (e.g., work, relationships) at the top; lifetime periods (‘when I was at university’); general events, repeated (‘weekly hockey’) or single extended (‘my trip to Australia’); and at the bottom episodic memories / event-specific knowledge: images, feelings and details. The working self holds current goals and self-images. It controls both encoding and retrieval, and prefers coherence (memories consistent with the self) over correspondence (accuracy). People even misremember their past selves as worse to feel they have improved (Newman & Lindsay, 2009).

Evidence: in retrograde amnesia, general events and lifetime periods are often preserved while specific episodes are lost; patient KC had no episodic memories but kept some general personal knowledge (Rosenbaum et al., 2005). Woike et al. (1999) showed goal-dependent recall: agentic people recalled agentic memories and communal people communal memories (e.g., 65% vs 90% for positive experiences). In depression people retrieve over-general memories (Liu et al., 2013), and greater specificity predicts recovery (Brittlebank et al., 1993).

Limitations: the model is complex and hard to test in full, it is not clear exactly how the working self and the knowledge base interact, and it does not fully specify how episodic and semantic information combine.

  • Listing the levels without explaining the working self.
  • Treating autobiographical memory as purely episodic.
  • No evaluation or limitations.

Part A · Autobiographical memory
🎯 Learning objective · A5
❓ The question this screen answers
A5
Which techniques are used to study autobiographical memory and with which limitations do they come?

🧭 In plain words: Name the main methods and, for each, a concrete limitation. The core problem to mention: accuracy of personal memories is usually hard to check.

  • Diary, cue words, targeted events, AMI, public events, imaging
  • Core problem: accuracy is hard to verify
  • Contamination by retelling and photos
  • Trade-off: control vs realism
🪝 Memory hook: Checking a personal memory is like fact-checking a friend’s holiday story when you weren’t there: you need their photos or someone else who was.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Every method trades verifiability against naturalness. The more real the memory, the harder it is to check.
Tap to open ▸

The diary technique records events as they happen and tests them later (Linton; Wagenaar, 1986). It allows accuracy to be checked, but it is effortful, samples only the events the diarist chooses to write down, and studies usually have one participant (the researcher).

The Galton–Crovitz cue-word technique asks people to recall a memory for each word (‘river’) and date it (Crovitz & Schiffman, 1974). It produces the retention function, but the dates and content often cannot be verified, and the memories sampled depend on the cues chosen.

Targeted event recall asks about checkable events such as the birth of a sibling (Usher & Neisser, 1993). Accuracy can be verified with parents, but only a few salient events are available, and memories may be contaminated by family stories and photos. This is the key limitation for childhood memories: we cannot tell if we remember the event or the retelling.

The Autobiographical Memory Interview (Kopelman, Wilson & Baddeley, 1990) probes personal facts and specific incidents for each life period, useful for patients, but it is laborious, and answers are checked against relatives when possible (Zola-Morgan, Cohen & Squire, 1983). Public-event tests (famous faces, news events) are easy to verify but knowledge varies between people and items age quickly. Neuroimaging and think-aloud methods show the process of retrieval, but the lab setting is artificial and the results are correlational. Online studies (Janssen & Murre, 2008) reach thousands of people but control is lower.

MethodWhat it gives youMain limitation
DiaryVerifiable recordEffortful; selective; n = 1
Cue wordsRetention functionUnverifiable; cue-dependent
Targeted eventsCheckable factsFew events; contamination
AMIClinical profileLaborious; needs informants
Public eventsEasy scoringKnowledge varies; items age
Imaging / think-aloudProcessArtificial; correlational
  • Listing methods without a limitation for each.
  • Forgetting the contamination problem (source confusion).
  • Not naming studies that used the method.

Part B · Amnesia and the kinds of memory
🎯 Learning objective · B1
❓ The question this screen answers
B1
What is the difference between implicit and explicit memory?

🧭 In plain words: Define both, give an example task for each, and show the classic evidence that they are separable.

  • Explicit = conscious recall/recognition
  • Implicit = influence without awareness
  • Amnesics: poor explicit, normal implicit (≈ 45% both groups)
  • Supports separate memory systems/processes
🪝 Memory hook: Typing your password without being able to say the letters out loud: your fingers remember implicitly.
★ KEY INSIGHT · You can know without knowing that you know. Implicit memory is proof that memory is more than what we can report.
Tap to open ▸

Explicit memory is conscious remembering: you know you are retrieving something from the past. It is measured with recall and recognition tests. Implicit memory is shown when earlier experience changes performance without conscious recollection. It is measured with indirect tasks such as word-stem or fragment completion, perceptual identification, priming, and skill learning (Matlin).

The classic evidence comes from amnesia. Warrington and Weiskrantz (1970) showed amnesic patients and controls a list of words. On explicit tests (recall, recognition), the patients were much worse. On an implicit test (identifying fragmented words), the two groups performed the same, about 45% correct. This has been replicated many times (e.g., Schacter et al., 1994; Roediger & Amir, 2005). Baddeley describes the amnesic syndrome as impaired episodic (explicit) memory with preserved working memory, semantic knowledge, intelligence and implicit learning. HM, for example, improved at mirror drawing without remembering having practised.

ExplicitImplicit
AwarenessConscious recollectionNo awareness of remembering
TestsRecall, recognitionWord-fragment/stem completion, priming, skills
In amnesiaSeverely impairedLargely spared
Also calledDeclarativeNon-declarative / procedural
  • Defining implicit memory as ‘unconscious memory’ without naming a task.
  • Forgetting the patient evidence.
  • Confusing implicit memory with forgetting.

Part B · Amnesia and the kinds of memory
🎯 Learning objective · B2
❓ The question this screen answers
B2
What does the phenomenon dissociation entail?

🧭 In plain words: Define a dissociation, explain why it matters (evidence for separate systems), and give several examples from amnesia research. Bonus: single vs double dissociation.

  • Variable affects one test, not another
  • Double dissociation = stronger evidence
  • Explicit/implicit, recall/recognition, episodic/semantic, antero/retrograde
  • Jon: recall ✗, recognition ✓ → recollection vs familiarity
🪝 Memory hook: If a power cut kills the lights but not the fridge, they must be on different circuits.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Dissociations are the neuropsychologist’s fingerprints: they reveal where one memory system ends and another begins.
Tap to open ▸

A dissociation occurs when a variable (a brain lesion, a manipulation) has a large effect on one kind of memory test but little or no effect on another (Matlin). If a patient is impaired on task X but normal on task Y, this suggests that X and Y depend at least partly on different processes or brain systems. A double dissociation (patient 1: X impaired, Y intact; patient 2: the reverse) is stronger evidence, because it rules out that Y is simply easier.

Examples: (1) Explicit vs implicit: amnesic patients are impaired on recall and recognition but normal on word-fragment completion (Warrington & Weiskrantz, 1970). (2) Recall vs recognition: Jon, who has developmental amnesia after hippocampal damage at birth, scores far below average on recall but in the normal range on recognition in the Doors and People test (Baddeley, Vargha-Khadem & Mishkin, 2001). This supports a split between recollection (hippocampus) and familiarity (perirhinal cortex; Aggleton & Brown, 1999). (3) Context vs item memory: Horner et al. (2012) found that hippocampal volume predicted memory for context but not for items. (4) Episodic vs semantic: KC lost personal episodes but kept general knowledge; Jon acquired good semantic knowledge despite poor episodic memory. (5) Anterograde vs retrograde: their severity is not correlated across patients (Shimamura & Squire, 1991). (6) Personal vs public events: De Renzi, Liotti and Nichelli (1987) described a patient who remembered personal events but not public ones.

  • Giving the definition without an example.
  • Confusing ‘dissociation’ in memory research with dissociation in clinical psychology.
  • Not explaining why a dissociation matters.

Part B · Amnesia and the kinds of memory
🎯 Learning objective · B3
❓ The question this screen answers
B3
What is source amnesia?

🧭 In plain words: Define source amnesia, give the key experiments, and explain it (context binding).

  • Fact remembered, source forgotten
  • Schacter et al. (1984) trivia study
  • Huppert & Piercy (1978): familiarity mistaken for recency
  • Explanation: hippocampus binds item + context
🪝 Memory hook: “I read somewhere that…”: the fact survived, the ‘somewhere’ did not.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Source amnesia shows that knowing something and remembering learning it are separate achievements.
Tap to open ▸

Source amnesia is remembering a piece of information while forgetting where or when it was learned. Schacter, Harbluk and McLachlan (1984) taught amnesic patients made-up facts about famous people (e.g., about Bob Hope’s favourite food). Patients could later recall some facts but often did not know that they had just learned them in the experiment, and attributed them to general knowledge or television.

Huppert and Piercy (1978) showed pictures on day 1 (some twice) and on day 2. When asked on which day a picture was shown, amnesic patients judged pictures seen twice on day 1 as coming from day 2: they used familiarity (how strong the memory feels) instead of recollecting the context. Similar effects are found in rats with hippocampal lesions (Winocur & Mills, 1970).

The explanation is a context-binding deficit: the hippocampus acts as ‘mnemonic glue’ that binds an item to its time and place. Without it, the item can survive (via familiarity or semantic memory), but the link to the episode is lost. Healthy people show milder source errors too, which is why we can believe a rumour while forgetting it came from an unreliable source.

  • Confusing source amnesia with retrograde amnesia.
  • No experiment described.
  • Not linking it to context/hippocampus.

Part B · Amnesia and the kinds of memory
🎯 Learning objective · B4
❓ The question this screen answers
B4
Which types of amnesia are there?

🧭 In plain words: Classify the types (anterograde, retrograde, plus childhood, developmental and source amnesia), give a defining feature and an example of each, and mention causes and theories.

  • Anterograde vs retrograde relative to damage
  • Ribot: recent memories most vulnerable
  • Plus childhood, developmental, source amnesia
  • Consolidation & interference (Dewar et al., 2009)
🪝 Memory hook: Anterograde = the recorder no longer saves new files. Retrograde = the most recent folders were corrupted.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The direction of amnesia is defined by time relative to the damage: anterograde looks forward, retrograde looks back.
Tap to open ▸

Anterograde amnesia is the inability to form new lasting episodic memories after brain damage, while working memory, semantic knowledge and implicit learning are spared. Examples: HM after bilateral medial temporal lobe removal, and Clive Wearing after encephalitis. Causes include damage to the hippocampus and related structures, Korsakoff’s syndrome, and early Alzheimer’s disease. Early explanations included interference (Warrington & Weiskrantz, 1970), faster forgetting and shallow processing, but the modern view is a failure of consolidation and context binding. Dewar et al. (2009) showed that interference early after learning hurts patients most; resting in a quiet dark room after learning improves their retention (Dewar, Cowan & Della Sala, 2010).

Retrograde amnesia is loss of memories from before the damage. It usually follows Ribot’s law: recent memories are lost more than old ones, because older memories are better consolidated. Patients such as L.T. could not access large parts of their past. Anterograde and retrograde amnesia often co-occur but their severity is not correlated (Shimamura & Squire, 1991).

Other types: childhood (infantile) amnesia, the normal absence of memories from the first years (Part A); developmental amnesia, severe episodic memory problems after hippocampal damage early in life, with good semantic memory and intelligence (Jon); and source amnesia, remembering facts without their origin (B3). Amnesic patients also struggle to imagine the future (Hassabis et al., 2007), suggesting the same system is used to construct past and future scenes.

TypeCore featureExample
AnterogradeNo new episodic memoriesHM, Clive Wearing
RetrogradeLost past memories (recent > old)L.T.; Ribot’s law
ChildhoodNo memories before ~3Everyone
DevelopmentalEarly hippocampal damage; semantic OKJon
SourceFact without its originSchacter et al. (1984)
  • Mixing up the direction of antero-/retrograde.
  • Only listing two types.
  • No patient examples.

Part C · Photos, memory and offloading
🎯 Learning objective · C1
❓ The question this screen answers
C1
What are transactive memories?

🧭 In plain words: Define transactive memory (Wegner), show it between people and between people and technology, and give benefits and costs.

  • Remember who/what knows, not the content
  • Couples divide memory labour (Wegner et al., 1991)
  • Extends to computers, notes, Internet
  • Benefit: frees resources; cost: dependence
🪝 Memory hook: You don’t know your best friend’s phone number, but you know your phone does.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Transactive memory makes a group smarter than its members, but only while the group, or the phone, is there.
Tap to open ▸

Transactive memory (Wegner, 1987) is a shared memory system in which people remember who knows what instead of storing everything themselves. Couples divide the labour of remembering: one partner remembers birthdays, the other bills. Wegner, Erber and Raymond (1991) showed that real couples remembered more than pairs of strangers when they could use their natural division of labour.

The idea extends to objects and technology. People remember less when they expect information to be saved on a computer, but remember where it is stored (Sparrow, Liu & Wegner, 2011); taking notes reduces memory for the noted content (Eskritt & Ma, 2014); and access to the Internet changes how much people try to know (Ferguson, McLean & Risko, 2015). Relying on external aids is called cognitive offloading (Risko & Gilbert, 2016).

The benefit is efficiency: offloading frees resources for other tasks (Storm & Stone, 2015). The cost is dependence: when the partner or device is unavailable, the information cannot be recalled. Henkel (2014) suggested the camera may act as such a partner, which leads to Part C.

  • Defining it as ‘memory of transactions’.
  • Only giving the couples example, not technology.
  • Forgetting the cost.

Part C · Photos, memory and offloading
🎯 Learning objective · C2
❓ The question this screen answers
C2
How does taking pictures affect our memory?

🧭 In plain words: Describe the photo-taking-impairment effect (Henkel, 2014) and the Soares & Storm (2018) experiments: design, results, and conclusion.

  • Photo-taking-impairment effect (Henkel, 2014)
  • Impairment even when photos disappear/deleted
  • Extra viewing time did not remove it (Exp 2)
  • People wrongly believe photos help
  • Photos help later only as retrieval cues
🪝 Memory hook: At a concert, the person filming the whole song often remembers it less than the person dancing.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The camera costs memory at the moment of taking the photo, not because we know the photo is saved.
Tap to open ▸

Henkel (2014) found that museum visitors remembered fewer objects and fewer details of objects they photographed than of objects they only observed: the photo-taking-impairment effect. Soares and Storm (2018) tested whether this is because people rely on the camera to remember for them.

Experiment 1 (n = 42, within-subjects): participants viewed 15 paintings for 15 s each, either observing, taking a photo with a camera app (photos saved), or taking a photo with Snapchat (photos disappear). After a 10-minute Tetris filler, a 30-item multiple-choice test on visual details was given. Memory was worse after using the camera than observing (≈ .45 vs .58; d = 0.70), and worst with Snapchat (≈ .36; d = 1.21 vs observe). So the impairment occurred even when photos would not be kept. A limitation: participants spent less time looking in the Snapchat condition, and may not have believed the photos would vanish.

Experiment 2 (n = 51) replaced Snapchat with a Delete condition (take a photo, then delete it) and gave participants the full 15 s of viewing after taking the photo. Observing still produced better memory (≈ .56) than Camera (≈ .49) and Delete (≈ .48), which did not differ. So even extra viewing time after the photo did not remove the cost.

A post-test survey showed that most participants believed photos help memory (52%), yet many of them remembered less, showing a metacognitive blind spot. The conclusion: taking a photo impairs memory for what was photographed, and this happens whether or not the photo is saved. Photos can still help later as retrieval cues when they are reviewed (e.g., SenseCam; Loveday & Conway, 2011), and freely chosen photography can increase engagement (Barasch et al., 2017).

Experiment 1Experiment 2
N4251
ConditionsObserve, Camera, SnapchatObserve, Camera, Delete
ResultObserve > Camera > SnapchatObserve > Camera = Delete
Main effectF(2,82) = 15.35, ηp² = .27F(2,100) = 4.26, ηp² = .08
  • Forgetting the Snapchat/Delete logic (the test of offloading).
  • Mixing up the design of the two experiments.
  • Stating photos always harm memory (reviewing them can help).

Part C · Photos, memory and offloading
🎯 Learning objective · C3
❓ The question this screen answers
C3
Which explanations exist for the effect photo taking has on our memory?

🧭 In plain words: Present the explanations (offloading, attentional disengagement, metacognitive illusion, implicit offloading) and use the Soares & Storm data to evaluate them.

  • Offloading: predicted no impairment in Snapchat/Delete → rejected
  • Attentional disengagement: fits data
  • Metacognitive illusion: possible
  • Implicit offloading: possible
  • Boundary: volitional vs instructed photos
🪝 Memory hook: It is not that your phone remembers for you; it is that your phone was looking and you were not.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The critical test is the Snapchat/Delete condition: if offloading were the cause, disappearing photos should not hurt memory. They did.
Tap to open ▸

(1) The offloading hypothesis (Henkel, 2014): people treat the camera as a transactive memory partner and stop encoding because ‘the camera remembers’. This predicts that the impairment should disappear when the photo will not be kept (Snapchat, Delete). It did not: impairment was as large or larger. So explicit offloading is not supported.

(2) The attentional-disengagement hypothesis: the act of taking a photo (framing, handling the phone) pulls attention away from the experience, and this disengagement continues after the camera is lowered. This fits both experiments, including Experiment 2 where extra viewing time did not help, and fits reports that people feel less engaged while photographing (Mols et al., 2015). It is supported, though any secondary task might have a similar effect.

(3) A metacognitive illusion: taking a photo creates a feeling of having encoded the scene (fluency), so people invest less effort afterwards (Bjork, Dunlosky & Kornell, 2013). This fits the survey result that people believe photos help memory. Possible.

(4) Implicit or automatic offloading: from years of experience, photographing has become linked with ‘stored elsewhere’, so people offload automatically even when they know the photo will vanish. Possible, and hard to rule out.

A boundary condition is important: when people freely choose what to photograph, photography can increase engagement and memory for visual details (Diehl, Zauberman & Barasch, 2016; Barasch et al., 2017). In the Soares & Storm studies photos were instructed. So the effect depends on how, and why, the photo is taken.

  • Only naming offloading.
  • Not using the data to evaluate each explanation.
  • Forgetting the boundary condition (volitional photography).

Resource A · Autobiographical memory
🧠 In-depth tutorial question · A1

Does the Galton-Crovitz cue-word technique involve direct and/or generative retrieval?

❓ Tutorial question A1
A1
Does the Galton-Crovitz cue-word technique involve direct and/or generative retrieval?

🧭 In plain words: Describe the technique, recall the two retrieval routes of the self-memory system, and decide which route(s) a cue word can trigger, with evidence.

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
SymptomA named method + ‘which retrieval route?’
DiagnosisSelf-memory system: generative vs direct retrieval.
TreatmentDescribe the method → define both routes → argue ‘both’ with Uzer et al. (2012).
  • Task: cue word → memory → describe → date
  • Instruction to search = generative set-up
  • Cue can also trigger a memory directly
  • Uzer et al. (2012): both, direct ~3× faster
  • Dating/describing adds generative elaboration
🪝 Memory hook: Asked ‘name a time you were proud’, sometimes you search your life story, sometimes a memory jumps out before you even start.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The technique is a generative task, but it does not guarantee a generative process: retrieval can take either route.
Tap to open ▸

In the Galton-Crovitz cue-word technique (Crovitz & Schiffman, 1974) participants are given a word (e.g., ‘river’ or ‘frustrated’), asked to retrieve an autobiographical memory associated with it, describe it briefly and date it (Robinson-Riegler). Collecting many memories and dates gives the retention function.

Conway and Pleydell-Pearce (2000) distinguish generative retrieval, a deliberate, effortful search guided by the working self (cue → lifetime period → general event → event-specific knowledge, with each candidate checked against the goal), and direct retrieval, in which a cue activates event-specific knowledge so that a memory comes to mind spontaneously.

The answer is both. Because participants are instructed to find a memory for each cue, the task is set up as a goal-directed search, so much of it is generative: people often have to think, ‘When did I feel frustrated? Maybe at university…’. But a cue word can also immediately call up a memory, which is direct retrieval. Uzer, Lee and Brown (2012) showed exactly this with the cue-word method: participants recalled memories to emotion words (e.g., frustrated, amused) while thinking aloud. Some memories were retrieved directly and others generatively; direct retrieval was about three times faster and involved much less vocalisation, as expected from an automatic process.

Two further points strengthen the answer: dating the event and describing it afterwards requires generative elaboration even when the memory itself popped up directly; and because the working self steers generative search, the technique samples memories that are relevant to current goals, not a random sample of life.

  • Answering only ‘generative’ without the direct route.
  • Not describing the technique.
  • No evidence (Uzer et al., 2012).

Resource A · Autobiographical memory
🧠 In-depth tutorial question · A2

A2 · The last part of the autobiographical retention function is referred to as ‘a st…

❓ Tutorial question A2
A2
The last part of the autobiographical retention function is referred to as ‘a standard forgetting curve’. Why do you think it is called that?

🧭 In plain words: Explain what the last part of the retention function shows, and why its shape matches the classic forgetting curve from memory research.

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘Why is it called…?’ about a curve’s name.
DiagnosisThe classic forgetting curve (Ebbinghaus) applied to the retention function.
TreatmentSay what the last segment shows → match its shape to the classic curve → give causes (no rehearsal, interference).
  • Last ~20 years of the retention function
  • More recent = more memories; decline with time since event
  • Same shape as the classic (Ebbinghaus) forgetting curve
  • Causes: decay, interference, less rehearsal
  • Childhood amnesia & bump are deviations from it
🪝 Memory hook: Your last week is sharp, last month is fuzzy, last year is patchy: the same curve Ebbinghaus drew for nonsense syllables.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The last part is ‘standard’ because it is the baseline: ordinary forgetting. The bump and childhood amnesia are what need special explanations.
Tap to open ▸

The retention function (Rubin, Wetzler & Nebes, 1986; Figure 7.1) shows how many memories older adults retrieve from each period of their life. It has three parts: childhood amnesia, the reminiscence bump (ages 10–30), and, for the most recent 20 years or so, a standard forgetting curve that is visible only in older participants.

It is called that because this part shows the same pattern as ordinary forgetting found in laboratory research since Ebbinghaus: the more time that has passed since an event, the fewer memories of it are recalled. If you read the last part of Figure 7.1 from right to left, from the present back into the past, the number of memories first drops steeply and then more slowly. That is the typical shape of a forgetting curve.

In other words, nothing special is going on in these years: recent events are remembered best because they are recent, and older ones are gradually lost through decay, interference from newer similar events, and lack of rehearsal (Wagenaar, 1986, found recall of diary events fell from about 75% to under a third over four years). This is exactly what makes the other two parts interesting: childhood amnesia (too few memories) and the reminiscence bump (too many) are departures from what a standard forgetting curve would predict.

  • Describing the curve without linking it to classic forgetting research.
  • Forgetting that the x-axis is age at encoding (read it backwards as time since the event).
  • Not saying why it is contrasted with the other two parts.

Resource A · Autobiographical memory
🧠 In-depth tutorial question · A3

A3 · Jack et al. (2009) found that adolescents with the earliest memories had enjoyed…

❓ Tutorial question A3
A3
Jack et al. (2009) found that adolescents with the earliest memories had enjoyed the most elaboration (relative to repetition) from their mother 10 years earlier. Do you think boys are more prominent among the elaboration or the repetition group?

🧭 In plain words: Use what Robinson-Riegler says about narrative style and the child’s sex to make a reasoned prediction. It is a prediction, so argue it.

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘Do you think…?’ asks for a reasoned prediction.
DiagnosisNarrative style linked to the child’s sex (Robinson-Riegler; Davis, 1999).
TreatmentState the link sex → style → earliest memory, predict, and add a caveat.
  • Prediction: boys in the repetition group
  • Daughters get elaborative talk; sons pragmatic talk
  • Elaboration → richer, earlier memories (Jack et al., 2009)
  • Female superiority in recall (Davis, 1999)
  • Style is the cause, not sex itself
🪝 Memory hook: ‘What was the best part of the zoo? What did the giraffe do? How did you feel?’ vs ‘Zoo was nice, wasn’t it?’
★ KEY INSIGHT · Memory talk is a social cause of autobiographical memory: how parents talk with a child shapes what the child can later remember.
Tap to open ▸

I would expect boys to be more prominent in the repetition group (low elaboration relative to repetition).

The reason comes from research on narrative style (Fivush, 1991; Reese & Fivush, 1993). When talking about past events with their daughters, parents tend to use an elaborative style: long, richly detailed conversations that add new information and ask open questions. With their sons, parents more often use a pragmatic style: short, succinct and with less detail and elaboration. Children of elaborative parents give better and more detailed accounts of past events, and Davis (1999) found evidence for female superiority in autobiographical recall (Robinson-Riegler).

Jack et al. (2009) found that the higher the ratio of elaborations to repetitions in mothers’ talk at age 2–4, the earlier the adolescents’ first memories 10 years later. If mothers elaborate more with daughters, girls should be overrepresented in the elaboration group and boys in the repetition group, and on average girls should have somewhat earlier first memories.

Two caveats show critical thinking. First, this is an inference: the readings do not report the sex split in Jack et al. Second, the causal factor is the style of talk, not the child’s sex: a boy whose mother elaborates a lot should also have early memories.

  • Just saying ‘boys’ without the narrative-style evidence.
  • Claiming the readings report the sex split.
  • Treating sex as the cause instead of parental style.

Resource A · Autobiographical memory
🧠 In-depth tutorial question · A4

A4 · Which of the factors invoked to explain childhood amnesia and the reminiscence b…

❓ Tutorial question A4
A4
Which of the factors invoked to explain childhood amnesia and the reminiscence bump are similar?

🧭 In plain words: Put the explanations of the two phenomena side by side and show which same factor appears in both, working in opposite directions (absent in infancy → few memories; peaking in early adulthood → many memories).

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
SymptomTwo phenomena, ‘which factors are similar?’
DiagnosisExplanations of childhood amnesia vs the reminiscence bump.
TreatmentLine up both lists → pick shared factors (brain, self/identity, language/narrative) → show opposite directions.
  • Brain: immature vs peak
  • Self: not yet formed vs being formed
  • Language & narrative: developing vs life story
  • Culture: offset vs life script
  • Same factors, opposite effects
🪝 Memory hook: Childhood: the camera isn’t built yet. Young adulthood: brand-new camera, and every scene is a ‘first’.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Both phenomena are about when the tools for storing a personal past are available: missing early, at their peak in young adulthood.
Tap to open ▸

The two phenomena sit at opposite ends of the retention function, but they are explained by overlapping factors:

  • Brain development / neurocognitive functioning. Childhood amnesia: the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex are still immature (Nadel & Zola-Morgan, 1984). Reminiscence bump: the peak-functioning account holds that the brain encodes best in adolescence and early adulthood (Janssen & Murre, 2008).
  • The self and identity. Childhood amnesia ends when a cognitive self develops that can organise experiences as happening to ‘me’ (Howe & Courage, 1997). The bump is explained by identity formation: events in these years define who we become and are kept by the self (Erikson; Habermas & Bluck, 2000; Conway, 2005).
  • Language, narrative and rehearsal. Childhood amnesia is linked to language development and memory talk with parents (Nelson, 1993; Reese & Fivush, 1993). The bump is linked to events being retold and rehearsed as part of the life story, and to the novelty and distinctiveness of ‘firsts’ that invites retelling.
  • Culture. The offset of childhood amnesia varies with culture (Wang, 2006). The bump is explained by the life script: culturally expected events (graduation, marriage) that cluster in early adulthood.

So the same ingredients (a working brain, a self, language and narrative, and a culture that tells us which events matter) explain both why early life is missing and why young adulthood is over-represented. Before they are in place we remember little; while they are developing fastest and events are self-defining, we store and rehearse a lot.

FactorChildhood amnesiaReminiscence bump
BrainImmature hippocampus/PFCPeak functioning (Janssen & Murre)
SelfNo cognitive self yet (Howe & Courage)Identity formation (Erikson; Habermas & Bluck)
Language / narrativeLanguage & memory talk (Nelson; Fivush)Life story, retelling, rehearsal
CultureOffset differs (Wang, 2006)Cultural life script
  • Listing explanations separately without pairing them.
  • Forgetting culture/life script.
  • Not explaining the opposite direction of the same factor.

Resource A · Autobiographical memory
🧠 In-depth tutorial question · A5

A5 · How do the notions of coherence and correspondence relate to the self-memory sys…

❓ Tutorial question A5
A5
How do the notions of coherence and correspondence relate to the self-memory system model?

🧭 In plain words: Define both notions, place them in the model (working self vs knowledge base), and explain Conway’s claim about which one wins over time, with an example.

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
SymptomTwo concepts + a model: ‘how do they relate?’
DiagnosisConway’s coherence vs correspondence within the self-memory system.
TreatmentDefine both → place them in the model (working self vs knowledge base) → which wins and an example.
  • Correspondence = accuracy (episodic detail)
  • Coherence = fit with goals & self-image (working self)
  • Conway (2005): coherence wins over time
  • Example: past selves remembered as worse (Newman & Lindsay, 2009)
  • Memory serves the self, not only accuracy
🪝 Memory hook: Your memory is an autobiography, not a CCTV recording: it keeps the scenes that fit the story.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The working self is the reason coherence wins: it is the gatekeeper for what is encoded and retrieved.
Tap to open ▸

In the self-memory system (Conway & Pleydell-Pearce, 2000; Conway, 2005) the working self (current goals and self-images) controls the encoding and retrieval of memories from the autobiographical knowledge base. Conway (2005) described two competing demands on these memories.

Correspondence means that memories are accurate: they correspond to what actually happened. It is served by episodic memories and event-specific knowledge, which hold sensory-perceptual detail close to the original experience.

Coherence means that memories are consistent with our current goals, beliefs and self-image. It is served by the working self and by the conceptual self (life story, themes, lifetime periods), which organise memories into a story that makes sense.

According to Conway (2005), we want both, but over time coherence tends to win out over correspondence. The working self shapes what is encoded, which memories are accessible, and how they are reconstructed, so memories drift toward what fits the current self. This makes autobiographical memories often inaccurate. For example, people claim that aspects of their lives (the self, a relationship) are better now than in the past, but this ‘improvement’ is often due to remembering their past selves in a negatively biased way (Newman & Lindsay, 2009). Such inaccuracies can protect self-image and social relationships.

So coherence and correspondence describe the trade-off at the heart of the model: autobiographical memory is organised for the self first, and for accuracy second.

  • Swapping the two definitions.
  • Not linking coherence to the working self.
  • No example or evidence.
