  • Negative: 47% agentic / 90% communal congruent
  • Working self = goals that steer retrieval
  • Correlational: supports, doesn’t prove
🪝 Memory hook: Ask a footballer and a friend group’s ‘glue’ for their best day ever: one describes a match, the other a birthday.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Same question, different memories: what we retrieve depends on who we are and what we want. That filter is the working self.
Tap to open ▸

The study. Woike et al. (1999) distinguished two personality types: agentic (emphasis on independence, achievement and personal power) and communal (emphasis on interdependence and similarity to others). Participants wrote about a positive or negative personal experience. For positive experiences, 65% of agentic participants recalled agentic memories (e.g., success) and 90% of communal participants recalled communal memories (e.g., love, friendship). The same pattern held for negative experiences: 47% of agentic individuals recalled agentic memories (e.g., failure), and 90% of communal individuals recalled communal memories (e.g., betrayal of trust).

The working self. In the self-memory system, the working self is a set of current goals and self-images that controls which information is encoded and which memories are retrieved. Memories relevant to our goals are more accessible; as Conway and Pleydell-Pearce put it, autobiographical memories are largely ‘records of success or failure in goal attainment’.

Why the result supports it. Agentic and communal people have different central goals (achievement vs relationships). If the working self filters retrieval by current goals, then the same open instruction (‘write about a positive experience’) should bring up goal-congruent memories: achievement for agentic people, relationships for communal people. That is exactly what was found. It suggests that retrieval is not random or driven only by what happened, but steered by a goal-based structure within the person: the working self.

Critical note. The finding is correlational (personality type was measured, not manipulated), and agentic people’s lives may simply contain more agentic events. Even so, the strong match between motives and recalled memories is what the working-self concept predicts, and it links to coherence (A5): memories that fit the self are the ones we keep and retrieve.

  • Describing the study without explaining the working self.
  • Getting the numbers wrong or omitting them.
  • Not mentioning that the design is correlational.

Resource B · Amnesia
🧠 In-depth tutorial question · B1

B1 · Watch the video clip. Which symptoms qualify this man as suffering from anterogr…

❓ Tutorial question B1
B1
Watch the video clip. Which symptoms qualify this man as suffering from anterograde amnesia?

🧭 In plain words: Use the definition of anterograde amnesia as a checklist: show (a) that he cannot form new lasting episodic memories after a brain injury, and (b) that other abilities are spared, which is what makes it a selective memory disorder rather than general confusion or dementia.

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
SymptomA video + ‘which symptoms qualify…?’
DiagnosisThe definition of anterograde amnesia as a checklist.
TreatmentTick lost (new episodes after injury) AND spared (WM, semantic, skills, intelligence).
  • Definition: can’t form new lasting episodic memories after brain damage
  • Forgets within minutes, repeats himself, disoriented
  • Spared: STM, language, intelligence, semantic memory, skills
  • Older, pre-injury memories largely intact
  • Onset after a specific brain event
🪝 Memory hook: His ‘record’ button is broken, but the ‘play’ button for old tapes and the live microphone still work.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The diagnosis rests on the contrast: new episodes are lost, but everything needed to use memory in the moment is still there.
Tap to open ▸

Anterograde amnesia is a problem in encoding, storing or retrieving new information after brain damage, typically to the hippocampus and related medial temporal structures (Baddeley et al.). In its pure form it involves impaired episodic memory with preserved working memory, semantic memory, implicit learning and intelligence. The symptoms that qualify the man in the clip are:

  • He forgets new events and people within minutes: someone he has just met, or something he has just done, is gone once his attention moves on. This is the core sign: new episodes are not stored in long-term memory.
  • He repeats questions and stories, because he does not remember having asked or told them.
  • He cannot say what happened earlier the same day and may be disoriented about the date, the place or why he is there.
  • His short-term memory is intact: he can follow a sentence and hold a normal conversation, so the problem is not attention or working memory.
  • His general knowledge, language and intelligence are intact, and he can often talk about his life before the injury (retrograde memory is less affected, especially for older memories, in line with Ribot’s law).
  • Skills and habits can still be learned (implicit/procedural memory), like HM improving at mirror drawing without remembering having practised.
  • The problem began after a clear brain event (e.g., surgery, encephalitis, oxygen loss, Korsakoff’s syndrome), which marks the ‘anterograde’ direction: memory fails from that point forward.

Together, a severe, selective loss of new explicit memory with spared short-term memory, intelligence and implicit learning qualifies him as having anterograde amnesia.

  • Listing only ‘he forgets things’ without the spared abilities.
  • Confusing anterograde with retrograde amnesia.
  • Not naming the brain cause or the link to the hippocampus.

Resource B · Amnesia
🧠 In-depth tutorial question · B2

B2 · Warrington and Weiskrantz (1970) showed a dissociation between explicit and impl…

❓ Tutorial question B2
B2
Warrington and Weiskrantz (1970) showed a dissociation between explicit and implicit memory. We encountered dissociations before in Problem 2. In which context?

🧭 In plain words: Recall where Problem 2 (short-term and working memory) used the same logic: one factor affects task X but not task Y, taken as evidence for separate memory systems.

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘We met X before: where?’ A link-back.
DiagnosisDissociation logic in Problem 2 (STM vs LTM).
TreatmentDefine dissociation → recall HM vs KF (double dissociation) → link.
  • Dissociation = factor affects one task, not the other
  • Problem 2: STM vs LTM (HM vs KF, double dissociation)
  • Serial position: delay kills recency, not primacy
  • Working memory: loop vs sketchpad in dual-task studies
  • Problem 3: explicit vs implicit (Warrington & Weiskrantz)
🪝 Memory hook: A light switch that kills the kitchen but not the living room tells you they run on different circuits.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Dissociations are the same argument in every chapter: if two abilities can break separately, they rely on different systems.
Tap to open ▸

In Problem 2 dissociations were used to argue that short-term and long-term memory are separate stores (the multi-store model), and that working memory has separate subsystems. The most likely contexts from your readings are:

  • Neuropsychological double dissociation between STM and LTM. Patient HM (after medial temporal lobe removal) had a normal digit span but could not form new long-term memories; patient KF (Shallice & Warrington, 1970) had a very poor digit span but could still learn new long-term information. Opposite patterns in two patients = a double dissociation, strong evidence for two separate systems.
  • The serial-position curve. A filled delay before recall removes the recency effect (items still in STM) but leaves the primacy effect (items transferred to LTM) intact, while slower presentation improves primacy but not recency (Glanzer & Cunitz, 1966). Each variable affects one part of the curve and not the other.
  • Working memory dual-task studies. A verbal secondary task (e.g., articulatory suppression) disrupts phonological-loop tasks but not visuospatial ones, and a spatial task disrupts the visuospatial sketchpad but not the loop. This dissociation is the basis for Baddeley’s separate components.

The link to Resource B: just as KF and HM showed that STM and LTM can fail independently, Warrington and Weiskrantz’s amnesic patients showed that explicit and implicit long-term memory can also come apart (poor recall and recognition, but normal fragmented-word completion, ≈ 45% in both groups).

  • Only saying ‘STM and LTM’ without an example or patient.
  • Describing a single dissociation as if it were double.
  • Not explaining why a dissociation is evidence for separate systems.

Resource B · Amnesia
🧠 In-depth tutorial question · B3

B3 · Huppert and Piercy (1978a, 1978b) found that amnesic patients were more likely t…

❓ Tutorial question B3
B3
Huppert and Piercy (1978a, 1978b) found that amnesic patients were more likely to say that items presented twice on day 1 had been presented on day 2; controls showed the opposite. How do these results show that binding item to context is a focal deficit in amnesia?

🧭 In plain words: Explain the task, the two cues people can use to answer ‘which day?’ (familiarity vs context), and why the patients’ reversed pattern means they have the item but not its context.

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
SymptomA reversed pattern + ‘how does this show…?’
DiagnosisFamiliarity vs context in source/time judgements.
TreatmentExplain task → two cues → patients use familiarity → so item kept, context lost.
  • Two cues for timing: context vs familiarity
  • Controls: repetition helps → more accurate ‘day 1’
  • Patients: repetition misleads → ‘day 2’
  • Items remembered, context lost → binding deficit
  • Same idea: source amnesia; hippocampus = ‘glue’
🪝 Memory hook: You know a song is familiar, but not whether you heard it this morning or ten times last year: familiarity has no time stamp; context does.
★ KEY INSIGHT · A reversal is more informative than a simple impairment: the same repetition helps one group and misleads the other, so the two groups must be using different information.
Tap to open ▸

The task. Participants saw pictures on day 1 (some shown twice) and on day 2 (shown once), then judged for each picture on which day it had been shown. There are two ways to answer. One is to recollect the context: to remember the episode in which the picture appeared (‘I saw that on the first day, in the morning session’). The other is to rely on familiarity: a general feeling of how strong the memory is. Familiarity is high for recent items, but also for items seen twice.

Controls had intact episodic memory, so they could link each picture to its day. Seeing a picture twice gave them a stronger item–context trace, so they were more accurate at assigning twice-shown pictures to day 1.

Amnesic patients still recognised the pictures, so their memory for the items was not gone. But they could not bind the item to its context (the day), so they had to fall back on familiarity. A picture seen twice on day 1 felt about as strong as, or stronger than, a picture seen once on day 2, and strong familiarity ‘feels recent’. So they misattributed it to day 2. As Baddeley et al. put it, without the link to context provided by episodic memory, they could not distinguish greater familiarity from two presentations from familiarity due to a recent experience.

Why this points to a binding deficit. The same manipulation (two presentations) helped controls but misled patients. The patients’ problem is therefore not a weak item memory in general, but a failure to link items to their time and place. The same pattern appears in source amnesia (Schacter et al., 1984: patients recall a trivia fact but not that they just learned it), in hippocampal lesions in rats (Winocur & Mills, 1970), and in Horner et al. (2012), where hippocampal volume predicted memory for context but not for items. The hippocampus acts as the ‘mnemonic glue’ that binds items to context.

ControlsAmnesic patients
Recognise the picture?YesYes (item memory present)
Cue used for ‘which day?’Context (recollection)Familiarity only
Effect of seeing it twice on day 1Stronger context link → more ‘day 1’Feels stronger = recent → ‘day 2’
ConclusionBinding intactItem–context binding fails
  • Saying patients ‘forgot the pictures’: they recognised them.
  • Not explaining why repetition makes the patients choose day 2.
  • Missing the link to the hippocampus and source amnesia.

Resource B · Amnesia
🧠 In-depth tutorial question · B4

B4 · In developmental amnesia, ‘remembering’ and ‘knowing’ are discussed. We encounte…

❓ Tutorial question B4
B4
In developmental amnesia, ‘remembering’ and ‘knowing’ are discussed. We encountered both notions in the readings for Problem 3A. In which context?

🧭 In plain words: First show you understand the distinction (recollection vs familiarity without recollection) and how it was used with Jon; then find where Problem 3A used the same remember/know judgements: in the study of childhood amnesia.

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
SymptomTwo terms + ‘where in Problem 3A?’
DiagnosisRemember/know: Jon (3B) and childhood amnesia (3A).
TreatmentDefine both → how Jon used them → Multhaup et al. (2005) in 3A.
  • Remember = re-experience; know = familiarity only
  • Jon: recognition OK, recollection lacking (Düzel et al., 2001)
  • 3A: Multhaup et al. (2005), childhood amnesia
  • Early memories ‘known’ → ‘remembered’ from ~4.7 years
  • Also: autobiographical memory vs autobiographical fact
🪝 Memory hook: You know you went to your 2nd birthday party because of the photo; you remember your 10th because you can still taste the cake.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Both readings use remember/know to separate re-living from knowing about the past, and both link re-living to a system that is not yet (childhood) or no longer (Jon) fully working.
Tap to open ▸

Remembering is recollecting an episode, mentally travelling back in time to re-experience it; knowing is recognising that something was encountered before, without re-experiencing the episode. In developmental amnesia, Jon (hippocampal damage at birth) had poor recall but near-normal recognition. When asked to classify his recognition as ‘remember’ or ‘know’, he used both categories about as often as controls, but his ‘remember’ responses lacked the brain signature of recollection (Düzel et al., 2001). This fits the proposal that recollection depends on the hippocampus and familiarity on the perirhinal cortex (Aggleton & Brown, 1999).

In Problem 3A the same distinction appeared in the context of childhood amnesia (Robinson-Riegler). Multhaup, Johnson and Tetrick (2005) asked adults to judge their memories of events from early childhood as ones they truly remember (re-experience) or only know about (e.g., from family stories or photos). Memories from the earliest years were mostly ‘known’; the proportion of ‘remembered’ memories rose with age, with childhood amnesia waning at about 4.7 years.

More broadly, 3A also linked the two notions to the episodic vs semantic parts of autobiographical memory: an autobiographical memory is re-experienced (remembering), whereas an autobiographical fact is simply known (knowing), and repeated episodes can turn from the first into the second.

  • Defining the terms but not naming the 3A study.
  • Mixing up which one depends on the hippocampus.
  • Forgetting that Jon’s ‘know’ responses were preserved.

Resource B · Amnesia
🧠 In-depth tutorial question · B5

B5 · People with memory problems undergo a variety of tests during neuropsychological…

❓ Tutorial question B5
B5
People with memory problems undergo a variety of tests during neuropsychological screening. How might this lead to an underestimate of the recall abilities of anterograde amnesiacs?

🧭 In plain words: Link testing practice to consolidation and interference: tests given in the delay between learning and recall act as interfering material, and amnesic patients are especially vulnerable to interference early in consolidation.

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
SymptomA practical setting + ‘how could this underestimate…?’
DiagnosisConsolidation and early interference (Dewar et al.).
TreatmentTests between learning and recall = interference → patients most vulnerable early → recall underestimated.
  • Screening = many tests in a row
  • Tests in the delay = interfering material
  • Amnesics: consolidation fragile, very sensitive to early interference
  • Quiet dark room: patients almost like controls (Dewar et al., 2010)
  • So scores underestimate true recall ability
🪝 Memory hook: It’s like testing whether wet cement holds a footprint while people keep walking over it.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The measurement changes what is measured: the battery itself causes forgetting in the patients it is meant to assess.
Tap to open ▸

In a typical screening session a patient learns something (e.g., a story or word list), then completes several other tests (digit span, naming, fluency, figure copying) before being asked to recall the first material. For a healthy person this filled delay matters little. For amnesic patients it matters a great deal.

New memories are initially fragile and need consolidation to become stable, a process that depends on the hippocampus and is most vulnerable in its early stages (Müller & Pilzecker, 1900). Della Sala’s group showed that amnesic patients are especially sensitive to interference during this window. In Dewar, Cowan and Della Sala (2010), four densely amnesic patients and six controls tried to recall a story after one hour. When the hour was spent resting in a quiet, dark room, the patients performed almost as well as controls. When the hour was filled with the sort of cognitive tasks that would normally constitute patient assessment, the patients remembered virtually nothing. Dewar et al. (2009) found that interference early after learning was most harmful for patients with mild cognitive impairment.

So a test battery creates the very interference that wipes out the patients’ recently learned material. Their low recall scores then reflect the testing situation as much as their true capacity: the battery underestimates what they could recall under interference-free conditions. Additional factors can add to this: fatigue and reduced motivation over a long session, and proactive interference when several similar tests (e.g., word lists) follow each other.

The practical implication: clinicians should build in interference-free rest after learning, and rehabilitation can use quiet rest to improve retention.

  • Only saying ‘patients get tired’.
  • Not naming consolidation and interference.
  • Missing the Della Sala / Dewar evidence.

Resource C · Soares & Storm (2018)
🧠 In-depth tutorial question · C1

C1 · Use the reading instructions to review the Soares and Storm (2018) article: IVs,…

❓ Tutorial question C1
C1
Use the reading instructions to review the Soares and Storm (2018) article: IVs, manipulation, DV, results, effect sizes, significance, causation and generalisation.

🧭 In plain words: Read the article like a researcher. Answer each of the seven sub-questions briefly and precisely, with the numbers from the paper.

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘Review the article’: a research-methods checklist.
DiagnosisDesign of Soares & Storm (2018): IV, DV, stats, causality, generalisation.
TreatmentAnswer each sub-question with numbers from the paper.
  • IV: photo condition (3 levels), manipulated within subjects
  • DV: proportion correct on 30 MC visual-detail items
  • Observe best; Snapchat (Exp 1) / Camera = Delete (Exp 2) worst
  • All key effects significant, d ≈ 0.5–1.2
  • Causal claim plausible; mechanism and generalisation limited
🪝 Memory hook: IV-DV-Result-Stats-Cause-Who: ‘I Don’t Really Study Causes Wrongly’.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The study shows that photo-taking impairs memory under controlled conditions; it does not yet show why, or how far it generalises.
Tap to open ▸

Independent variable(s). One IV per experiment: photo-taking condition, with three levels. Experiment 1: Observe, Camera (photo saved in the photo album), Snapchat (photo sent and not saved). Experiment 2: Observe, Camera, Delete (photo taken and immediately deleted, followed by 15 s of viewing).

Manipulated? Within or between? Yes, it was manipulated by the researchers, within participants: every participant did all three conditions, each on a block of five paintings. A Latin square counterbalanced which paintings went with which condition and the order of the conditions; in Experiment 2 participants were randomly assigned to the counterbalancing orders.

Dependent variable and measurement. Memory for visual details of the paintings: a 30-item multiple-choice test (two questions per painting, four options each, chance = .25), given after a 10-minute Tetris filler task, scored as proportion correct by an experimenter blind to condition.

Highest and lowest; effect sizes. Experiment 1: Observe highest (≈ .58), Camera (≈ .45), Snapchat lowest (≈ .36). Camera < Observe, d = 0.70; Snapchat < Observe, d = 1.21; Snapchat < Camera, d = 0.48; overall ηp² = .27. Experiment 2: Observe highest (≈ .56), Camera (≈ .49) and Delete (≈ .48) lowest and not different from each other. Camera < Observe, d = 0.58; Delete < Observe, d = 0.61; overall ηp² = .08. These are medium to large effects.

Statistically significant? Yes. Experiment 1: F(2, 82) = 15.35, p < .001, and all three planned comparisons (p = .003, p < .001, p = .031). Experiment 2: F(2, 100) = 4.26, p = .017; Camera vs Observe p = .026, Delete vs Observe p = .005; Camera vs Delete not significant, t(50) = 0.25, p = .80.

Conditions of causation. (1) Covariation: memory differs across conditions. (2) Temporal order: the condition was manipulated before memory was measured. (3) Alternative explanations: the within-subjects design controls individual differences; counterbalancing controls painting difficulty and order; scoring was blind; Experiment 2 equalised viewing time and made ‘no access’ believable. So the authors make it plausible that the photo-taking procedure causes the impairment. What is not settled is which part of the procedure (handling the phone, the switch between tasks, a metacognitive illusion). In Experiment 1, less viewing time in the Snapchat condition was a confound, which Experiment 2 fixed.

Generalisation. The authors generalise to people photographing experiences in daily life (‘for a truly memorable experience… it might sometimes be best to put the camera away’). This is only partly convincing. Support: the effect replicates Henkel’s (2014) museum field study. Limits: small samples of UCSC undergraduates doing it for course credit; paintings on a screen in a lab; instructed rather than self-chosen photos; a short 10-minute delay; a test only of visual details; photos were never reviewed. Volitional photography can even improve visual memory (Barasch et al., 2017).

Experiment 1 (n = 42)Experiment 2 (n = 51)
IV levelsObserve, Camera, SnapchatObserve, Camera, Delete
DesignWithin; Latin squareWithin; Latin square; random assignment to orders
Viewing time15 s including photo15 s after the photo
Means (≈).58 / .45 / .36.56 / .49 / .48
Overall testF(2,82) = 15.35, p < .001, ηp² = .27F(2,100) = 4.26, p = .017, ηp² = .08
Key dCam–Obs 0.70; Snap–Obs 1.21; Snap–Cam 0.48Cam–Obs 0.58; Del–Obs 0.61; Cam = Del
  • Calling the design between-subjects.
  • Giving means without effect sizes or stats.
  • Accepting the generalisation without naming sample, setting and instructed photos.

Resource C · Soares & Storm (2018)
🧠 In-depth tutorial question · C2

C2 · Provide alternative examples of transactive memories between people, and between…

❓ Tutorial question C2
C2
Provide alternative examples of transactive memories between people, and between people and devices.

🧭 In plain words: Give your own examples (not only Wegner’s couples) that show the core idea: you remember who or what knows the information, and rely on it.

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘Give examples of…’
DiagnosisTransactive memory between people and with devices.
TreatmentOwn examples: who/what knows, and you rely on it.
  • Remember who/what knows, not the content
  • People: family, work team, friends, siblings
  • Devices: contacts, calendar, search engine, navigation
  • Benefit: frees resources; cost: dependence
🪝 Memory hook: Your brain keeps the index; the phone keeps the book.
★ KEY INSIGHT · A good example always has two parts: the information is stored elsewhere, and you know where.
Tap to open ▸

Transactive memory (Wegner, 1987) is a shared memory system in which people store information in each other, or in objects, and remember who or what knows what.

Between people:

  • In a family, one parent keeps track of school dates and the other of dentist appointments; each knows to ask the other.
  • In a work team, you don’t memorise the payroll rules because you know Anna does, and IT questions go to Tom.
  • Friends on holiday: one remembers the name of the restaurant, the other the route back to the hotel.
  • Siblings who each hold different parts of family history and together reconstruct a story.

Between people and devices:

  • You no longer know phone numbers by heart, but you know your contacts app has them.
  • Appointments live in a calendar app, so you stop rehearsing them (and forget them if the phone dies).
  • For facts, you remember where to find them (a search engine) rather than the fact itself (Sparrow, Liu & Wegner, 2011).
  • Navigation apps hold the route, so you learn less of the city layout.

In each case the benefit is freed-up capacity (Storm & Stone, 2015); the cost is that the information is hard to recall when the partner or device is unavailable.

  • Examples of simply forgetting, without relying on a partner.
  • Only repeating Wegner’s couples.
  • No benefit/cost.

Resource C · Soares & Storm (2018)
🧠 In-depth tutorial question · C3

C3 · What would Figure 1 of Soares and Storm (2018) look like if the offloading accou…

❓ Tutorial question C3
C3
What would Figure 1 of Soares and Storm (2018) look like if the offloading account of the photo-taking-impairment effect were correct?

🧭 In plain words: Derive a prediction from the offloading hypothesis and draw it: which bars go up, which stay down?

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘What would the figure look like if…?’
DiagnosisDeriving a prediction from the offloading account.
TreatmentOffloading → no-save bar back at Observe level → draw and contrast with actual data.
  • Offloading: impairment only if the photo is available later
  • Prediction: Observe ≈ Snapchat/Delete > Camera
  • Actual: Snapchat/Delete ≤ Camera
  • So offloading is not supported
🪝 Memory hook: If you know the notebook will be burned, you don’t rely on it; so memory should be back to normal. It wasn’t.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The decisive bar is the third one: it is the condition where offloading is impossible.
Tap to open ▸

The offloading hypothesis (Henkel, 2014) says that people remember photographed objects less because they count on the camera to remember for them. It therefore predicts impairment only when people expect to be able to use the photo later.

  • Observe: highest, as in the real data.
  • Camera (photo saved): lower than Observe, because people offload onto the saved photo. This matches the real data.
  • Snapchat (Exp 1) and Delete (Exp 2): the photo cannot be used later, so there is nothing to offload to. Memory should be about as good as Observe, and at least clearly better than Camera.

So the third bar in each experiment would rise back up to (or near) the Observe bar, leaving Camera as the only low bar. In the real figure the opposite happened: the Snapchat bar was even lower than Camera (≈ .36 vs .45) and Delete equalled Camera (≈ .48 vs .49). This pattern contradicts the offloading account and supports attentional disengagement.

  • Drawing all bars equal.
  • Predicting that Camera would be as good as Observe.
  • Not comparing the prediction with the real figure.

Resource C · Soares & Storm (2018)
🧠 In-depth tutorial question · C4

Which of the two experiments has the strongest design? Why?

❓ Tutorial question C4
C4
Which of the two experiments has the strongest design? Why?

🧭 In plain words: Compare the experiments on internal validity: which one rules out more alternative explanations? Name the specific confounds that Experiment 2 fixed.

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘Which design is strongest? Why?’
DiagnosisInternal validity and confounds (time, belief).
TreatmentName confounds in Exp 1 → show how Exp 2 fixes them → note remaining limits.
  • Both: within-subjects, Latin square
  • Exp 2 equalised (even increased) viewing time
  • Exp 2 made ‘no access’ certain (Delete)
  • Exp 2 power analysis: n ≥ 49 for 90%
  • Stronger design ≠ larger effect
🪝 Memory hook: Experiment 1 asked the question; Experiment 2 closed the loopholes.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The strongest design is the one that leaves the fewest alternative explanations, not the one with the biggest effect.
Tap to open ▸

Experiment 2 has the stronger design. Both experiments are within-subjects and counterbalanced with a Latin square, but Experiment 2 removes the two weaknesses the authors themselves identified in Experiment 1:

  • Viewing time. In Experiment 1 the photo had to be taken within the 15 s, so photo conditions had less looking time, and Snapchat probably took longer to use than Camera. In Experiment 2 the 15 s of viewing started only after the photo was taken (and deleted), so photo conditions had equal or even more total exposure. The impairment still appeared, which rules out ‘less looking time’.
  • Believability of the manipulation. Participants may not have fully believed that Snapchat photos would be unavailable. In the Delete condition participants deleted the photo themselves, so they knew it was gone.
  • Sample size. Experiment 2 used a power analysis based on Experiment 1 (n ≥ 49 for 90% power), with n = 51 and random assignment to counterbalancing orders.

Experiment 1 did produce a larger effect (ηp² = .27 vs .08), but a larger effect in a design with confounds is less convincing than a smaller effect in a cleaner design. One remaining limitation of Experiment 2 is that only 31 of 51 participants completed the survey, but this does not affect the main result.

  • Choosing Experiment 1 because the effect was bigger.
  • Not naming the time confound.
  • Forgetting the power analysis.

Resource C · Soares & Storm (2018)
🧠 In-depth tutorial question · C5

C5 · Participants who took and deleted a photo, then observed the painting for as lon…

❓ Tutorial question C5
C5
Participants who took and deleted a photo, then observed the painting for as long as Observe participants, still remembered it less. How do the authors explain this? Could it also be a task-switching effect?

🧭 In plain words: Give the authors’ explanation(s) of this ‘prospective’ impairment, then evaluate a task-switching account and say how you could test it.

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘How do the authors explain…? Could it also be…?’
DiagnosisMetacognitive illusion / implicit offloading vs task switching.
TreatmentGive authors’ accounts → evaluate task-switching → propose a test.
  • Impairment continues after the camera is put down
  • Authors: disengagement via metacognitive illusion or automatic offloading
  • Alternative: task-switch cost / attention residue
  • Authors admit any secondary task might do it
  • Test: non-photo secondary task of equal duration
🪝 Memory hook: After answering a text, you ‘look’ at the lecture slide again, but your mind is still half on the phone.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The Delete finding rules out time but not task: it shows the cost is in what the photo does to the mind, not in how long you look.
Tap to open ▸

The authors’ explanation. The finding shows that photo-taking does not only disrupt encoding while the photo is taken, but prospectively impairs encoding after the camera is put down. The authors favour attentional disengagement that continues after the photo, and offer two speculative mechanisms: (1) a metacognitive illusion: taking the photo gives a feeling of encoding fluency, so participants think they have already encoded the painting and invest less effort in the following 15 s (Bjork, Dunlosky & Kornell, 2013; Koriat, 1993); and (2) automatic (implicit) offloading: through years of experience, photographing has become linked with ‘this is stored elsewhere’, so people encode less even when they consciously know the photo is deleted. They also note that any secondary task might cause disengagement, which future research should test.

Could it be task switching? Yes, this is a plausible alternative. In the photo conditions participants had to switch from one task (operating the phone: framing, taking, deleting, pressing the spacebar) to another (studying the painting). Task switching carries switch costs: time and control are needed to reconfigure for the new task, and attention may remain partly on the previous task (attention residue). This could reduce encoding at the start of the 15 s. A problem for this account is that classic switch costs last only a short time, while viewing lasted 15 s; still, attention residue could last longer, and the authors themselves admit that any secondary task might produce the effect.

How to test it. Add a condition with a secondary task that also requires switching but involves no photo (e.g., typing the painting’s title on the phone, or a tone-counting task) of the same duration. If memory is impaired as much as in the Delete condition, a general task-switching/secondary-task account is supported; if photo-taking impairs memory more, there is something specific about photographing (such as the metacognitive illusion).

  • Only repeating ‘attentional disengagement’ without the mechanisms.
  • Answering yes/no to task switching without explaining or testing it.
  • Forgetting that viewing time was equal (or longer).

Resource C · Soares & Storm (2018)
🧠 In-depth tutorial question · C6

C6 · Why would it be incorrect to conclude on the basis of this study that taking pic…

❓ Tutorial question C6
C6
Why would it be incorrect to conclude on the basis of this study that taking pictures creates less memorable experiences?

🧭 In plain words: Show the gap between what was measured and the broad claim. Name concrete limits of the DV, the task, the sample and the photo situation.

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘Why would it be incorrect to conclude…?’
DiagnosisGeneralisation and construct validity limits.
TreatmentContrast measured DV with the broad claim → list limits of DV, task, sample, photo situation.
  • DV = visual details only, not the experience
  • 10-min delay; photos never reviewed
  • Instructed vs volitional photos (Barasch et al., 2017)
  • Lab paintings, student sample
  • Relative impairment, not ‘unmemorable’
🪝 Memory hook: Measuring one ingredient and judging the whole meal.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Always match the claim to the measure: ‘less memory for visual details after 10 minutes’ is not ‘less memorable experiences’.
Tap to open ▸

The conclusion goes far beyond the data, for several reasons:

  • Narrow DV. The study measured recognition of visual details of paintings on a multiple-choice test. A ‘memorable experience’ also includes gist, emotions, enjoyment, meaning and the social context, none of which were measured.
  • Short retention interval, no photo review. Memory was tested after 10 minutes, without access to the photos. In real life photos can act as powerful retrieval cues later (SenseCam: Berry et al., 2007; Loveday & Conway, 2011), so photographed experiences may be remembered better in the long run, provided people actually look at their photos.
  • Instructed, not volitional photos. Participants were told what to photograph. When people choose what to photograph, it can increase engagement and memory for visual aspects (Diehl, Zauberman & Barasch, 2016; Barasch et al., 2017), and automatic wearable cameras had no effect (Niforatos et al., 2017).
  • Artificial experience. Paintings on a computer screen in a lab are not a holiday, a concert or a wedding; ecological validity is limited.
  • Sample. Small groups of UCSC undergraduates participating for course credit.
  • Relative, not absolute. The finding is that photographed paintings were remembered less than observed ones, not that the experience was not memorable.

So the correct conclusion is narrower: under these lab conditions, being instructed to take a photo reduces short-term memory for visual details of the photographed object.

  • Only saying ‘small sample’.
  • Missing the volitional-photography evidence.
  • Forgetting that photos can help later as retrieval cues.

Robinson-Riegler & Robinson-Riegler, pp. 268–279 · Eysenck & Keane, pp. 314–320 · Problem 3a

Block A · Autobiographical Memory

❓ How is memory for our own lives organised, why does it have the shape it has, and what does it reveal about the self?

📈A.1

What Autobiographical Memory Is, and the Shape of a Remembered Life

❓ This lecture answers: What exactly is a life memory, how can you study one, and how are memories spread across a lifetime?
A.1.1
A memory versus a fact about yourself

🏫 Re-lived event = autobiographical memory (episodic); plain fact about you = autobiographical fact (semantic). Repetition shifts memories from episodic to semantic.

A.1.2
How do you study a life?

🔍 Targeted event recall (checkable events), diary technique (known accuracy), Galton–Crovitz cue-word technique (Crovitz & Schiffman, 1974): samples the whole lifespan.

A.1.3
The retention function: the shape of a remembered life

📈 Rubin, Wetzler & Nebes (1986): gap before ~3 (childhood amnesia), hill at 10–30 (reminiscence bump), rise for the last ~20 years (forgetting curve).

INTERACTIVE · THE CUE-WORD TECHNIQUE ON YOURSELF

🔤 Five cue words, five memories, your own curve

For each cue word, think of one specific memory and type how old you were. The bars show your mini retention function. illustrative five memories is far too few for a real curve.

QUICK SORT

🏫 Memory or fact?

🎞️
THINK OF IT LIKE…A film versus its plot summary. An autobiographical memory is a scene you can replay; an autobiographical fact is a line in the plot summary. Watch the same scene a hundred times (the walk to school) and only the summary is left.
✗ THE MISTAKEExplaining the recent rise with a short-term memory store, like the recency effect in a word list (Theme 2).
✓ CORRECTThe autobiographical rise covers decades, so it is a long-term effect: simply the tail of an ordinary forgetting curve.
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDThere’s remembering and there’s knowing. And if you graph how many memories people have from each age, it always looks the same: nothing from being a baby, loads from your teens and twenties, and a pile of recent stuff.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKRe-live it = memory; just know it = fact. Gap, hill, rise.
✎ EXAM TIPLearn the three features with their ages: before ~3, 10–30, the last ~20 years. Exam questions like to swap them.

📚 All studies and details in this lecture: Robinson-Riegler: memory shifts from episodic to semantic with repetition (links to Linton, 1975, and Baddeley’s semantic memory as residue of episodes). Targeted event recall uses events that can be corroborated; the diary technique lets researchers check accuracy; the cue-word technique asks for a memory, a short description and a date.

▶ Find a video: the shape of autobiographical memory
✅ Quick check: does the cue-word technique involve direct or generative retrieval? (Canvas A.1)

Mainly generative: you deliberately search for a memory that fits the cue, using your working self. Sometimes a cue triggers a memory straight away (direct retrieval).

👶A.2

Childhood Amnesia: When Does a Life Story Begin?

❓ This lecture answers: Why do adults remember almost nothing from their first years?
A.2.1
The puzzle, and how to study it

❓ Toddlers learn constantly but adults remember almost nothing. Usher & Neisser (1993): checkable events; poor before 5; sibling birth and hospitalisation reach further back than a move or a death.

A.2.2
Explanation 1 — The brain is not ready

🧠 Immature hippocampus and PFC; procedural before declarative. But 2–3-year-olds recall events from age 1–2 (Bauer, 2004), so this explains only the first months.

A.2.3
Explanation 2 — Language and memory talk

🗣️ Language leaps at 2–4 (Pillemer & White, 1989). Elaborative style with daughters, pragmatic with sons; Nelson (1993): memory talk, parents as “play-by-play announcers”.

A.2.4
Explanation 3 — A sense of self

🪞 Howe & Courage (1997): language expresses memories, the sense of self organises them. No “me”, no memory about me.

A.2.5
Explanation 4 — Culture and parenting

🌏 Wang (2006): U.S. adults’ earliest memories earlier and more autonomous than Taiwanese; mother cue early in both. Jack et al. (2009): more maternal elaboration → earlier first memory.

A.2.6
Explanation 5 — It all comes together: the social-cognitive account

✨ Nelson & Fivush (2004): explicit memory, narrative, memory talk, consciousness of the past (~4), theory of mind emerge gradually. Multhaup et al. (2005): ≈ 4.7 years.

INTERACTIVE · WHICH EXPLANATION FITS?

🧩 Match the finding to the explanation

Tap a finding to see which explanation it supports (or challenges).

INTERACTIVE · JACK ET AL. (2009): READING A NEGATIVE CORRELATION

🗣️ Slide the mother’s elaboration-to-repetition ratio

Direction from the study; the exact ages are illustrative.

Elaboration : repetition ratio: medium
🧶
THINK OF IT LIKE…Knitting a scarf. You need yarn (a brain that stores), needles (language), a pattern (a sense of self) and someone showing you how (memory talk). The scarf doesn’t appear at one moment; it grows row by row.
✗ THE MISTAKE“A negative correlation in Jack et al. means more elaboration leads to worse memory.”
✓ CORRECTThe measure is the age of the earliest memory. A lower age is better, so more elaboration means earlier memories.
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDNobody remembers being two. Not because the brain can’t store anything, but because you need words, a sense of being ‘you’, and parents who talk with you about what happened. Those come together slowly, so real memories start somewhere between 2 and 5.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKBrain, Language, Self, Culture → Emergence.
✎ EXAM TIPA gradual, variable shift from ‘know’ to ‘remember’ memories → the social-cognitive account (Nelson & Fivush, 2004), with Multhaup et al.’s ≈ 4.7 years.

📚 All studies and details in this lecture: Usher & Neisser (1993): four checkable events (sibling birth, family move, death, hospitalisation); start age differed by event; for events at 3 or younger, family stories and photos went with fewer memories, at 4–5 they made memories stronger. “Emergence of autobiographical memory” and “offset of childhood amnesia” describe the same process. Brain: Nadel & Zola-Morgan (1984), Squire (1987), Diamond & Doar (1989), Bachevalier & Mishkin (1984), Schacter & Moscovitch (1984), Bauer et al. (2000), Bauer (2007). Language: biggest leaps at ages 2 and 4; narrative style (Fivush, 1991; Reese & Fivush, 1993); Davis (1999); Nelson (1993): generic event memory for repeated events and an autobiographical memory system for unique ones. Self: Howe, Courage & Edison (2003). Culture: independent (U.S.) vs interconnectedness (Taiwan; Lu & Gilmour, 2007; Markus & Kitayama, 1991); Wang (2006) cue words self, mother, family, friend, surroundings, scored for autonomy; relationships matter everywhere, their relative importance differs. Jack et al. (2009): prospective; mothers’ elaborations vs repetitions about six events; strong negative correlation with age of earliest memory. Also MacDonald et al. (2000); Peterson et al. (2009); Wang & Ross (2007). Emergence: Bauer (2004); extended consciousness (Povinelli et al., 1999); theory of mind; end placed at 2–2.5 (Eacott & Crawley, 1998) or ~5 (Wetzler & Sweeney, 1986).

▶ Find a video: childhood amnesia
✅ Quick check: are boys more likely to be in the elaboration or the repetition group? (Canvas A.3)

The repetition group: parents tend to use a pragmatic, short style with sons and an elaborative style with daughters (Fivush, 1991; Reese & Fivush, 1993), and Davis (1999) found females better at autobiographical recall.

🎸A.3

The Reminiscence Bump and Forgetting

❓ This lecture answers: Why do we remember ages 10–30 so well, and why do recent ordinary days fade?
A.3.1
The bump: more than a collection of ‘firsts’

🎸 Firsts are memorable, but the bump also appears for preferences and public knowledge: songs (Holbrook & Schindler, 1989), books (Larsen, 1996), films (Schulster, 1996), Academy Awards (Rubin et al., 1998).

A.3.2
Four explanations

🧪 Cognitive mechanisms, identity formation, peak functioning, life script. Janssen & Murre (2008), ~3,500 people aged 16–75: bump unrelated to novelty, emotion, valence or importance. Brain: necessary and sufficient for the bump.

A.3.3
Forgetting: the third feature

📉 Wagenaar (1986): ≈75% → <33% over four years. Causes: lack of rehearsal, interference, routine; repeated episodes become facts (Linton, 1975). Culture: specific vs generic memories (Wang, 2009).

INTERACTIVE · MATCH THE FINDING TO THE ACCOUNT

🎯 Which account does each finding support?

🎧
THINK OF IT LIKE…Your all-time favourite playlist. Most of it is from your teens and twenties, not because those songs were better, but because that’s when your brain was recording at full quality and you were deciding who you are.
✗ THE MISTAKE“The bump is just because early adulthood is full of firsts.”
✓ CORRECTThe bump also appears for songs, books, films, public events, and for ordinary, neutral memories (Janssen & Murre, 2008), so firsts are not necessary.
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDYour twenties stick because lots was new, you were becoming you, your brain was at its best, and society says that’s when big stuff happens. One study even found boring memories from then stick, so the brain seems key. Normal days just blur together.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKFirsts, Self, Peak, Script.
✎ EXAM TIPJanssen & Murre → peak functioning; positive > negative → life script; unexpected events bump → identity (Conway, 2005).
▶ Find a video: the reminiscence bump
✅ Quick check: which factors explain both childhood amnesia and the bump? (Canvas A.4)

The development of the self: childhood memories are stored once a sense of self exists (Howe & Courage), and early-adult memories are strengthened while identity forms (Erikson; Habermas & Bluck). Brain development matters for both too: necessary but not sufficient for the end of childhood amnesia, necessary and sufficient for the bump.

📚A.4

A Theory of the Whole System: Conway’s Self-Memory System

❓ This lecture answers: How is a life stored, and how does the self decide what we remember?
A.4.1
How a life is stored: the knowledge base

📚 Conway & Pleydell-Pearce (2000): lifetime periods → general events → event-specific knowledge. Conway (2005): conceptual self + episodic memories, plus life story and themes; a network.

A.4.2
The working self: memory serves your goals

🎯 Goals shape storage and recall: memories are “records of success or failure in goal attainment”. Coherence vs correspondence: coherence tends to win (Newman & Lindsay, 2009).

A.4.3
Two routes to a memory

🛤️ Generative (deliberate, via the working self) vs direct (cue-triggered). Direct is 3× faster (Uzer et al., 2012), more specific but less identity-related (Johannessen & Berntsen, 2010); PFC vs left hippocampus (Addis et al., 2012).

A.4.4
Evidence and evaluation

🧪 Retrograde amnesia spares general levels; KC (Rosenbaum et al., 2005); self-knowledge survives (Klein & Lax, 2010). Woike et al. (1999): memories follow motives. Strengths: hierarchy, self, goals; limits: brain, “how”, episodic/semantic mix.

INTERACTIVE · ZOOM INTO A LIFE

🔍 Chapter → scene → detail

Tap each level to zoom in. illustrative example.

“My student years in Rotterdam”: a long stretch defined by an ongoing situation.
“Thursday evenings at the sports club” (repeated) or “the summer trip to Lisbon” (single).
The smell of rain on the court, a friend laughing as the ball hit the net: images and feelings lasting seconds to hours, in time order.
📕
THINK OF IT LIKE…An autobiography whose author is still alive. The chapters and scenes are on file, but today’s author (the working self) chooses which pages to open and quietly edits them so the story stays consistent with who she is now.
✗ THE MISTAKE“Every memory is retrieved by the working self.”
✓ CORRECTOnly generative retrieval goes through the working self. Direct retrieval is triggered by a cue and bypasses it: faster, more specific, less tied to identity.
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDYour memory is organised like a book about you: chapters, scenes, details. And the ‘you’ of today decides which pages you open and how you tell them, so memory often prefers being consistent over being correct.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKChapter → scene → detail; the working self holds the pen.
✎ EXAM TIPEvaluation: three strengths (hierarchy, self–memory link, goals) and three limits (brain complexity, the ‘how’ of interaction, episodic vs semantic mix).

📚 All studies and details in this lecture: Conway & Pleydell-Pearce (2000, p. 266): “Autobiographical memories are primarily records of success or failure in goal attainment.” Woike et al. (1999): agentic (independence, achievement, power) vs communal (closeness); positive experiences 65% vs 90%, negative 47% vs 90%. Strengths: hierarchical structure, link between memory and the self, role of goals, generative–direct distinction. Retrieval routes: Uzer et al. (2012) think-aloud with emotion words; Johannessen & Berntsen (2010); Addis et al. (2012).

▶ Find a video: Conway’s self-memory system
✅ Quick check: how do coherence and correspondence relate to the model? (Canvas A.5)

Correspondence = accuracy; coherence = fit with the working self’s current goals and beliefs. Conway (2005) says memory wants both, but over time coherence tends to win, so memories drift in self-serving ways (e.g., remembering past selves as worse; Newman & Lindsay, 2009).

🌧️A.5

The Brain Behind a Life Story, and What Depression Does to It

❓ This lecture answers: Which brain networks build life memories, and how does depression change them?
A.5.1
Brain networks of autobiographical memory

🧠 Medial/ventromedial PFC and temporal cortex nearly always active (Svoboda et al., 2006); real vs imagined: vmPFC + posterior cingulate (Summerfield et al., 2009); amygdala for emotional memories (Buchanan et al., 2006); four networks (St Jacques et al., 2011).

A.5.2
Depression: when the life story turns vague and fragmented

🌧️ Over-general memories (Liu et al., 2013); predict symptoms (Stange et al., 2013), specificity predicts recovery (Brittlebank et al., 1993). Affect regulation: avoidance (Debeer et al., 2011). Dalgleish et al. (2011): negative, compartmentalised life story.

QUICK SORT · SPECIFIC OR OVER-GENERAL?

🎯 A specific memory = one event, under one day

COMPARE · DALGLEISH ET AL. (2011)

📖 The life story in three groups

Direction of results from the study; bar heights are illustrative.

🌫️
THINK OF IT LIKE…Looking at old photos through frosted glass. A depressed person sees “bad times with people” instead of a sharp picture of one Tuesday. The frost may protect against painful detail, but it also hides the good scenes.
✗ THE MISTAKE“Vague memory causes depression.”
✓ CORRECTMost evidence is correlational. Only longitudinal findings (Stange et al., 2013; Brittlebank et al., 1993) show that specificity predicts later symptoms and recovery.
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDRemembering your life takes a team of brain networks. When people are depressed, their memories go vague, like ‘bad times with people’, probably because specific sad memories hurt. Getting specific again goes together with getting better.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKAll four networks build it; ‘me’ and ‘memory’ fill it in. Depression blurs and breaks the story.
✎ EXAM TIPKnow which two networks also elaborate (medial PFC + MTL), and separate correlational (Liu et al.) from predictive evidence (Stange; Brittlebank).

📚 All studies and details in this lecture: Task: a specific memory = an event lasting less than one day; reduced memory specificity in depression. Over-general memory predicted increases in symptoms eight months later in adolescents exposed to family emotional abuse (Stange et al., 2013); increasing specificity predicted recovery from major depression (Brittlebank et al., 1993). Affect regulation = a cognitive avoidance strategy (Debeer et al., 2011: threat instructions, avoidant coping). Dalgleish et al. (2011): current MDD, remitted, controls listed lifetime periods (9–10 on average); measures: proportion negative, compartmentalisation, positive redundancy, negative redundancy. Depressed: more negative, more compartmentalised, less integrated self (low positive redundancy); remitted in between, suggesting relapse risk. Brain: Markowitsch & Staniloiu (2011) amygdala for real, not fictitious, material.

▶ Find a video: over-general memory in depression
✅ Quick check: what is the affect regulation hypothesis?

Over-general memory as cognitive avoidance: specific negative memories bring intense emotion, so people avoid retrieving them. Debeer et al. (2011): threat instructions increased over-general memories, but only in people high in avoidant coping.

Baddeley, Eysenck & Anderson, pp. 438–445 · Matlin, pp. 146–147 · Problem 3b

Block B · Amnesia

❓ What do people with amnesia lose, what do they keep, and why?

⏪B.1

Amnesia: Two Directions of Loss

❓ This lecture answers: What are the two kinds of amnesia, who are the famous cases, and what memory survives?
B.1.1
Anterograde and retrograde amnesia

⏪⏩ Amnesia = severe episodic deficits (Buckner, 2010). Anterograde: no new memories; retrograde: old ones lost, worst just before the damage (Meeter & Murre, 2004). L.T. (Conway & Fthenaki, 2000).

B.1.2
The famous patients

🏥 H.M.: 1953 surgery removed temporal lobe parts and the hippocampus; classic anterograde case (sources differ on his old memories: “far from perfect”). Amnesic syndrome spares working, semantic, implicit memory, intelligence.

B.1.3
What survives: implicit memory

🧩 Warrington & Weiskrantz (1970): patients far worse on recall/recognition, but both groups ≈ 45% on mutilated-word guessing. A classic dissociation.

INTERACTIVE · WHICH AMNESIA?

🩺 Diagnose each case

COMPARE · WARRINGTON & WEISKRANTZ (1970)

🧩 Explicit vs implicit

Implicit scores are real data (≈ 45% both groups); explicit bars show only the direction (“much worse”), illustrative.

📼
THINK OF IT LIKE…A video recorder. Retrograde amnesia is a damaged library of old tapes; anterograde amnesia is a broken record button. And even with a broken record button, the machine still “warms up” faster for things it has handled before (implicit memory).
✗ THE MISTAKEThinking ‘anterograde’ means losing old memories, because ‘ante’ sounds like ‘before’.
✓ CORRECTAnterograde = forward from the injury: no new memories. Retrograde = backward: old memories lost.
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDThere are two kinds of amnesia: you either lose your past or you can’t make new memories from now on, and you can have one without the other. But even people who can’t remember a word list still guess the half-erased words as well as anyone.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKRetro = rewind broken; antero = record broken; implicit keeps working.
✎ EXAM TIPDefine ‘dissociation’ precisely (a variable affects one test strongly and another not at all), then apply it to Warrington & Weiskrantz.
▶ Find a video: anterograde amnesia▶ Find a video: patient H.M.
✅ Quick check: where did we meet dissociations before? (Canvas B.2)

In Theme 2, short-term (working) vs long-term memory: some patients have normal short-term but poor long-term memory, others the reverse. Together that is a double dissociation, evidence for separate systems.

🧷B.2

Explaining Amnesia: Context, Jon and Consolidation

❓ This lecture answers: What is the core deficit in amnesia, what does Jon show, and why do new memories need time to set?
B.2.1
The core deficit: linking events to their context

🧷 Amnesia breaks the item–context link (rats: Winocur & Mills, 1970). Huppert & Piercy (1978): twice-seen day-1 pictures judged day 2. Source amnesia (Schacter et al., 1984). Imagining futures (Hassabis et al., 2007).

B.2.2
Baddeley’s modal model, and the case of Jon

👦 Modal model: “mnemonic glue”, recall and recognition share storage, semantic = residue of episodes. Jon breaks all three: good semantic memory and intelligence, normal recognition, poor recall; ‘remember’ by strength.

B.2.3
Is Jon special? Recall versus recognition in the brain

🧠 Most patients lose both (Reed & Squire, 1997). Early damage? Spared perirhinal cortex? Aggleton & Brown (1999); adult case (Mayes et al., 2002). Horner et al. (2012): hippocampal volume predicts context, not item memory.

B.2.4
Consolidation: new memories need time to set

⏳ Traces start fragile (Müller & Pilzecker, 1900). Sleep helps; a quiet dark hour lets patients nearly match controls (Dewar et al., 2010); early interference hurts most (Dewar et al., 2009), via LTP.

B.2.5
Retrograde amnesia: how do you measure a lost past?

📜 Severities not correlated (Shimamura & Squire, 1991). Famous faces → Ribot’s law; public-event scales; checked recollections; AMI (Kopelman et al., 1990). De Renzi et al. (1987): personal kept, public lost.

INTERACTIVE · HUPPERT & PIERCY (CANVAS B.3)

📅 Picture seen twice on day 1: which day was it?

Choose who is answering.

INTERACTIVE · WHEN DOES INTERFERENCE HURT MOST?

⏳ Place the interference in the 9-minute delay

Dewar et al. (2009): patients with MCI kept only about 10% after early interference, more after later interference; controls were much less affected. Other values are illustrative.

TAP TO REVEAL · HOW DO YOU TEST A LOST PAST?

📜 Four methods for retrograde amnesia

🧱
THINK OF IT LIKE…Wet cement with a date stamp. Amnesia breaks the stamp (no “when and where”), so anything familiar feels recent. And fresh cement needs quiet minutes to set: walk on it early and the print is ruined.
✗ THE MISTAKE“Amnesic patients just forget faster, so they forget everything equally.”
✓ CORRECTThe most likely core problem is binding items to their context: familiarity can survive while ‘when and where’ fails (Huppert & Piercy; Horner et al., 2012).
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDAmnesia breaks the label that says when and where something happened, so patients think anything familiar must be recent. A guy called Jon can’t recall things but can recognise them, probably because a neighbouring brain area handles ‘seen it before’. And new memories are like wet cement: disturb them early and they’re gone.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKGlue, Jon, Set, Ribot.
✎ EXAM TIPFor Jon, list the three problems for the modal model. For consolidation, cite Müller & Pilzecker (1900) for the idea and Dewar et al. (2009) for ‘early is worst’.

📚 All studies and details in this lecture: early accounts: interference (Warrington & Weiskrantz, 1970), faster forgetting (Huppert & Piercy, 1979), shallow processing (Cermak, Butters & Moreines, 1974); Winocur (1978); Bob Hope trivia and source amnesia (Schacter, Harbluk & McLachlan, 1984); mental time travel (Tulving); Mullally & Maguire (2013). Jon: Vargha-Khadem et al. (2001); Doors and People Test (Baddeley, Vargha-Khadem & Mishkin, 2001b); Düzel et al. (2001); Maguire et al. (2001); Gardiner et al. (2008); Manns & Squire (1999). Horner et al. (2012): 17 patients, 14 controls, MEG, early 350 ms hippocampal signal. Sleep: Stickgold, James & Hobson (2000); Gaskell & Dumay (2003). Consolidation is the neurobiological level. Dewar, Cowan & Della Sala (2010): 4 densely amnesic patients and 6 controls recalled a story after an hour in a darkened, quiet room vs filled with tests; patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) benefited similarly. Dewar et al. (2009): word list tested after 9 minutes, interference in the first, second or third part; cellular mechanism: long-term potentiation (LTP). Retrograde vs anterograde severities not highly correlated, so different origins; the tester does not control the original learning; famous faces: earlier memories were better preserved; AMI tests personal semantic memory; De Renzi et al.’s patient kept her personal life but had no public events (source cut off there). Baddeley & Wilson (1986); Greene & Hodges (1996); Sanders & Warrington (1971); Ribot (1882); Squire, Haist & Shimamura (1989); Zola-Morgan, Cohen & Squire (1983); Korsakoff patients accurate on the AMI.

▶ Find a video: developmental amnesia▶ Find a video: consolidation
✅ Quick check: where did remember vs know appear in 3A? (Canvas B.4)

In Multhaup, Johnson & Tetrick (2005): childhood memories shift from ‘know’ to ‘recollect’, with the wane of childhood amnesia at about 4.7 years. It also mirrors autobiographical facts (knowing) vs autobiographical memories (re-living).

✅ Quick check: why might test batteries underestimate amnesic patients’ recall? (Canvas B.5)

Tests run back-to-back fill the minutes after learning with interference, exactly when consolidation is most fragile. Dewar et al. (2010) showed patients recall far more after a quiet, dark hour than after an hour of typical assessment tasks.

Soares & Storm (2018), Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition, 7, 154–160 · Problem 3c

Block C · The Photo-Taking-Impairment Effect

❓ Why does taking a photo of something make you remember it worse: because you trust the camera, or because photographing pulls your attention away?

📸C.1

Forget in a Flash: The Photo-Taking-Impairment Effect

❓ This lecture answers: Is the photo-taking-impairment effect caused by offloading or by attentional disengagement?
C.1.1
The effect and two explanations

📸 Henkel (2014): photographed museum objects remembered worse. Offloading (camera as prosthetic memory; transactive memory, Wegner, 1987) predicts no impairment for unsaved photos; attentional disengagement predicts impairment anyway.

C.1.2
Experiment 1: Snapchat

👻 42 students, within-subjects; Observe, Camera, Snapchat; 15 paintings, 15 s, 10-min Tetris delay, 30 questions. Camera < Observe (d = 0.70), Snapchat < Observe (d = 1.21), Snapchat < Camera (d = 0.48).

C.1.3
Experiment 2: Delete

🗑️ 51 students (power analysis: ≥ 49); photo then delete; 15 s viewing after the photo. Camera (d = 0.58) and Delete (d = 0.61) < Observe; Camera = Delete (p = .80). Only 19% think photos hurt memory.

C.1.4
What it means, and what it does not mean

🧭 Rules out explicit offloading; fits disengagement that lingers. Mechanisms: metacognitive illusion of fluency, or implicit offloading. Limits: told what to shoot; volitional photos can help (Barasch et al., 2017).

INTERACTIVE · WHAT WOULD EACH THEORY PREDICT? (CANVAS C.3)

🔮 Pick a theory to redraw Experiment 2

QUICK POLL · DOES TAKING PHOTOS HELP YOUR MEMORY?

🗳️ Your guess, then the survey

TAP TO REVEAL · DESIGN CHECK (CANVAS C.1, C.4)

🔬 Variables and the stronger experiment

🎤
THINK OF IT LIKE…Filming a concert on your phone. You’re looking at a small screen instead of the stage. Even after you lower the phone, part of you is still in ‘camera mode’, half-watching, as if the moment were already saved.
✗ THE MISTAKE“Offloading plays no role at all.”
✓ CORRECTOnly explicit offloading is ruled out. An implicit, automatic offloading habit may still exist, and may even be how disengagement happens.
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDTaking a photo makes you remember the thing worse. And it’s not because your phone remembers for you: people forgot just as much when the photo vanished on Snapchat or was deleted straight away. Taking the photo pulls you out of the moment, and you keep half-watching even after you put the phone down.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKDeleted photo, same damage: it’s the attention, not the storage.
✎ EXAM TIPLearn the prediction logic: offloading says unsaved photos shouldn’t hurt; disengagement says they should. Then state the result and that Experiment 2 fixed time and belief.

📚 All studies and details in this lecture: photos as retrieval cues (Berry et al., 2007; Loveday & Conway, 2011; St Jacques & Schacter, 2013); von Restorff effect (Von Restorff, 1933; Wallace, 1965); deeper encoding (Craik & Lockhart, 1972); prosthetic memory (Henkel, 2014; Risko & Gilbert, 2016); transactive memory (Wegner, Guiliano & Hertel, 1985; Wegner, Erber & Raymond, 1991); notes (Eskritt & Ma, 2014), computers (Sparrow, Liu & Wegner, 2011), Internet (Ferguson, McLean & Risko, 2015); benefits (Storm & Stone, 2015); manual vs automatic photos (Niforatos et al., 2017); disengagement felt (Mols et al., 2015). Exp. 1: F(2, 82) = 15.35, ηp² = .27; means ≈ .58/.45/.36. Exp. 2: F(2, 100) = 4.26, ηp² = .08; means ≈ .56/.49/.48; survey of 31: 52% helps, 26% no effect, 3% no guess, 19% impairs; 62.5% of believers still worse. Fluency (Bjork, Dunlosky & Kornell, 2013; Hertzog et al., 2003; Koriat, 1993); engagement (Diehl, Zauberman & Barasch, 2016); photos rarely reviewed (Whittaker, Bergman & Clough, 2010); Russell Banks.

▶ Find a video: the photo-taking-impairment effect
✅ Quick check: give examples of transactive memory (Canvas C.2)

Between people: one partner remembers birthdays, the other the finances; a team member who knows the IT system. Between people and devices: phone contacts instead of memorised numbers, calendar reminders, saved notes, search engines.

✅ Quick check: why not conclude that photos make experiences less memorable? (Canvas C.6)

The study tested memory for visual details of paintings, 10 minutes later, in a lab, with assigned photos. It says nothing about the experience as a whole, emotional meaning, long-term memory, volitional photography (which can increase engagement) or later reviewing photos as retrieval cues.

🧵 Synthesis: a life memory is built from three ingredients

IngredientWhat goes wrong without itEvidence
🪞 A self to organise itChildhood amnesia; a vague, fragmented story in depressionHowe & Courage; Nelson & Fivush; Conway; Dalgleish et al.
🪪 A forming identity and a peak brain(when present) the reminiscence bumpHabermas & Bluck; Janssen & Murre
🧷 A context tag (hippocampus)Amnesia: familiarity without recollection; source amnesiaHuppert & Piercy; Jon; Horner et al.
⏳ Time to consolidateEarly interference wipes new memoriesMüller & Pilzecker; Dewar et al.
👀 Attention at encodingPhoto-taking-impairment effectHenkel; Soares & Storm
A memory of your life is built, not recorded: it needs an experience properly encoded with attention, a context tag that binds it to a time and place, and a self that organises it.

📄 Theme 3 on one page

📈A1

What it is

Re-living a moment = autobiographical memory; just knowing it = fact. Count memories by age → gap, hill, rise.
👶A2

Childhood amnesia

Almost nothing before ~3, because brain, language, memory talk, self and theory of mind come together gradually (≈ 4.7 years).
🎸A3

Bump & forgetting

Ages 10–30 over-remembered (firsts, identity, peak brain, life script), even dull events. Recent days fade by routine and interference.
📚A4

Self-memory system

Chapters → events → details; the working self decides what is recalled; coherence beats accuracy; generative vs direct retrieval.
🌧️A5

Brain & depression

Four networks build memories (mPFC + MTL elaborate). Depression → vague, negative, fragmented memories; specificity predicts recovery.
⏪B1

Two amnesias

Anterograde = no new memories (H.M.); retrograde = old ones lost; separate. Implicit learning survives (45% vs 45%).
🧷B2

Why amnesia happens

Lost context glue; Jon: recall gone, recognition normal; consolidation needs quiet early minutes; Ribot: oldest memories last.
📸C1

Photo-taking

Photographed things are remembered worse, even when the photo is deleted or unsaved: disengaged attention, not offloading.
💬 The whole theme to a friend: “You don’t record your life like a video, you build it like a story about yourself. You need to be paying attention when it happens, your brain has to stamp it with a time and place, and you need a ‘me’ to hang it on. Take away one of those, whether you’re a toddler, an amnesia patient or someone filming a concert, and the memory doesn’t make it.”
